articles.title: The Download: AI agent tracking and climate feedback loops
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time

—Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance.

AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, from hacking websites to accessing private government files. In many cases, they’ve eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability .

​​In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. Because right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools.

Here’s what needs to change .

Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot

Climate change itself increasingly fuels climate change. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up global temperatures, creating dangerous feedback loops that aren’t fully represented in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming. Now, a growing number of observations and studies are indicating how powerful these cascading effects could be. By extension, they’re also showing how much faster the planet may warm this century.

Read more about the dangerous feedback loops accelerating global warming .

—James Temple

This article is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

Are we there yet? Solid-state batteries

Lithium-ion batteries power everything from personal electronics to grid-scale energy storage, but their liquid electrolytes have drawbacks, not least a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer.

The technology promises faster charging, longer life, greater energy density and improved safety, and a new generation of companies aims to bring it to market. If their bets pan out, the tech could ease the shift away from fossil fuels.

Find out how close solid-state batteries are to delivering on their promise .

—Alexander C. Kaufman

This story is part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue .

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers
Including undercover ICE agents. ( Wired $)
+ Much of the data relates to Customs and Border Protection. ( TechCrunch )
+ It also linked the agencies to specific surveillance tools. ( Reuters $)
+ Big Tech is pushing back against ICE’s demands for user data . ( WSJ $)
+ Activists want ChatGPT users to quit over ICE ties. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 Putin says Russia is coordinating with “genius” Musk on satellites
He said the cooperation maintains order in orbit. ( Bloomberg $)
+ ​​Russia is developing its own version of Starlink. ( Guardian )
+ Moscow added Apple and Microsoft to a surveillance registry. ( Quartz )
+ Here’s all the stuff we’ve put up in space. ( MIT Technology Review )

3 Apple just announced its first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen
It joins a blitz of product launches under new CEO John Ternus. ( CNN )
+ Steve Jobs and Tim Cook had both dismissed the idea. ( NYT $)
+ Executives say touchscreen advances mean it’s now worthwhile. ( Wired $)

4 Bloomberg and trading firms are paying to get Trump’s posts faster
They’ve signed up for Truth Social’s pay-for-access plan. ( Reuters $)

5 As US ties fray, Europe is planning its first subsea cable to Greenland
It will bypass the US to link Canada, Japan, and South Korea. ( Ars Technica )
+ The EU’s AI champion says Europe can rival US tech giants. ( FT $)

6 Palantir’s defense chief says AI could make China target Taiwan
He says Beijing may act to stop the US pulling ahead in AI. ( Bloomberg $)
+ Taiwan’s “silicon shield” could be weakening. ( MIT Technology Review )

7 Musk’s xAI has offered to buy homes if residents drop a noise lawsuit
The suit targets noise from powering its Mississippi data centres. ( Guardian )

8 The world’s first spinal cord transplant has sparked controversy
Experts say there’s little evidence the operation will work. ( New Scientist $)

9 China’s tech giants are fighting for attention with AI microdramas
Tencent and ByteDance are battling over the booming market. ( SCMP )
+ Chinese microdramas are AI content machines. ( MIT Technology Review )

10 Astronomers have spotted a possible new dwarf planet beyond Pluto
The icy world would be the solar system’s sixth dwarf planet. ( Gizmodo )

Quote of the day

“ They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.”

—A hacking group explains why it leaked personal information from the US Department of Homeland Security, NPR reports .

One more thing

How the Pentagon is adapting to China’s technological rise

It’s been just over a year since Kathleen Hicks stepped down as US deputy secretary of defense.

As the highest-ranking woman in Pentagon history, Hicks shaped US military posture through an era defined by renewed competition between powerful countries and a scramble to modernize defense technology.

In this conversation with MIT Technology Review , Hicks reflects on how the Pentagon is adapting—or failing to adapt—to a new era of geopolitical competition. She discusses China’s technological rise, the future of AI in warfare, and her signature initiative: Replicator.

Check out the full interview .

—Caiwei Chen

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ Astronomers have found a green star 280 light-years from Earth.
+ A Scottish labrador that detects “sea vomit” has won the Animal of the Year award.
+ England’s iconic Sycamore Gap is showing signs of new life three years on from its felling.
+ From Lime-bike jousting to chainmail-wearing pop stars, youth culture is embracing the medieval era .

articles.title: Winnie Ho 'willing to take political responsibility'
articles.excerpt: Winnie Ho, who resigned as secretary for housing over the Wang Fuk Court fire, said she was willing to bear…

Winnie Ho, who resigned as secretary for housing over the Wang Fuk Court fire, said she was willing to bear political responsibility for the deadly blaze.

In a statement, Ho said she met with Chief Executive John Lee on Wednesday and tendered her resignation, which Lee accepted.

Ho also said the government's reform measures, based on the independent committee's report, demonstrate a strong determination to confront the complex and longstanding problems exposed by the fire.

"Since July 1, 2022, I have fought side by side with the Housing Bureau team, working hard to reverse the longstanding housing problems that have plagued Hong Kong for years," she said.

Ho also listed achievements during her tenure, including the rapid construction of light public housing, shortening waiting times for public housing, tackling substandard subdivided units and clamping down on public housing abuse.

She said she felt deeply honoured to have served Hong Kong over the past four years, and expressed gratitude to the central government, the chief executive and the entire government team for their trust and support.

Ho also said she hopes those who were killed in the blaze can rest in peace and their families can move forward and recover from their grief.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: Plenum adopts resolution on Party self-governance
articles.excerpt: The Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee has adopted a resolution on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance…
articles.fullText:
The Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee has adopted a resolution on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance as it concluded its fifth plenary session, according to Xinhua News Agency.

The Politburo presided over the meeting.

President Xi Jinping, who's also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, delivered an important address, and a communique was issued after the session.

At the session, participants considered and adopted the Resolution of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China on Certain Major Issues concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance.

Xi delivered explanatory remarks on the draft of the resolution.

The CPC Central Committee gave a highly positive assessment of the great achievements the Party has made in exercising full and rigorous self-governance in the new era, Xinhua reported.

"It was stressed that many favourable conditions are now in place for advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance, while we also face many new circumstances and new issues in this endeavour," the communique said.

Profound changes in global, national and Party conditions have made the CPC's tasks of uniting and leading the people in safeguarding China's sovereignty, security, and development interests, of uniting and leading the people in promoting reform and development and maintaining social harmony and stability, and of maintaining its advanced nature and integrity even more formidable, it added.

Systematic plans for persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance were also made at the session, according to the communique.

Strict management of officials is the key to full and rigorous Party self-governance, it noted.

"We will build up the ranks of high-calibre officials with firm political commitment, outstanding professional competence, excellent work conduct, and strict discipline," it added.

Party organisations at all levels play the principal role in exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance, said the communique, adding that it is therefore essential to systematically advance the development of Party organisations at all levels and in all sectors to strengthen their political and organisational functions.

"It was noted that taking integrated steps to ensure that officials do not have the audacity, opportunity, or desire to commit corruption is both an important strategy for full and rigorous Party self-governance and a fundamental guideline for our fight against corruption," the communique said.

"We must take systematic steps to address both symptoms and root causes of corruption and adopt a holistic approach that combines severe punishment, targeted remedy, and effective prevention, carrying this fight through to the end."

Strengthening Party regulations and institutions represents a long-term, fundamental strategy for ensuring full and rigorous Party self-governance, said the communique.

The CPC Central Committee decided at the session that the Party will convene its 21st National Congress in Beijing in the second half of 2027 and stated that this congress, which is to be held at a critical stage for basically realising socialist modernisation and on a new journey toward the Second Centenary Goal, will be a highly important meeting and an event of great political significance for both the Party and the country.

The session elected Zhang Shengmin as a new Politburo member.

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
articles.excerpt: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment…
articles.fullText:
This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.

AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.

Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today.

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine , we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability : the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.

Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.

With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.

The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken.

Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from.

Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it.

OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized . The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people.

Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used.

No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.

AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist.

Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.

No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too.

Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance.

Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

articles.title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
articles.excerpt: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off…
articles.fullText:
Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs , and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.

None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March , which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.

Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.

At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project , through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.

But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.

So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story ). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.

Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.

Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.

The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

articles.title: HK stocks fall as Samsung chip result weighs on region
articles.excerpt: Mainland stocks ended lower on Thursday as a deepening selloff in tech shares overshadowed the US Federal Reserve's decision to…
articles.fullText:
Mainland stocks ended lower on Thursday as a deepening selloff in tech shares overshadowed the US Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates unchanged.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index fell 136 points, or 0.6 percent, to 22,958 on turnover of HK$189.45 billion.

The tech index dived 109 points, or 2.8 percent, to 3,744 while the China Enterprises Index slipped 35 points, or 0.5 percent, to 7,755.

On the mainland, the Shanghai Composite Index closed down 30 points, or 0.82 percent, at 3,651 on turnover of 715.62 billion yuan while the blue-chip CSI300 index fell one percent.

The Shenzhen Component Index plunged 334 points, or 2.92 percent, to 11,138 on turnover of 840.89 billion yuan while tech shares were among the main drags, with the startup board ChiNext Composite index ChiNext Index diving 117 points, or 4.45 percent, to 2,517 on turnover of 419.35 billion yuan. Shanghai's tech-focused Star50 index tumbled 4.3 percent to notch the weakest close since September 2025.

CSI 5G communications, which tracks 5G communications companies, plunged 7.4 percent.

Robot maker Yushu Technology, also known as Unitree, slumped 4.8 percent after its third-quarter net profit fell despite revenue rising 70 percent from a year earlier in its first earnings report since listing.

"Valuations for the tech AI hardware names are now close to the historical trough and imply a major deceleration in EPS growth ahead," said James Wang, head of China strategy at UBS Investment Bank Research.

"We are wary that investor sentiment on AI is fragile; however, we believe the risk-reward is looking more attractive again, and interest may come back towards the end of the year as investors rebuild their portfolios for the new year."

The Fed held interest rates steady, as expected, on Wednesday, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week's US midterm elections while it awaits further data on inflation, which the central bank said "remains elevated".

In Tokyo, the Nikkei ended 705 points, or 1.1 percent, higher at 64,659 in a volatile session that began with gains before briefly turning negative. The broader Topix index also reversed early losses to end the day up 11 points, or 0.29 percent, at 4,003.

In Seoul, the Kospi fell 74 points, or 1.24 percent, to 5,937 as the shares of chip giant Samsung Electronics dived over a lack of fresh shareholder-return plans and an outlook that lagged rival SK hynix's despite posting a 15-fold jump in quarterly profit. (Reuters & Xinhua)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Five-year plan 'all about finding new growth engines'
articles.excerpt: Financial Secretary Paul Chan said on Thursday Hong Kong's first five-year plan provides a clear framework for policymaking and investment…
articles.fullText:
Financial Secretary Paul Chan said on Thursday Hong Kong's first five-year plan provides a clear framework for policymaking and investment, urging businesses to understand the government's strategies and priorities so they can "plan and invest with confidence".

Speaking at a business forum, Chan highlighted two connected priorities – finance, and innovation and technology – in the plan, which was unveiled last month.

"For Hong Kong, we are equally determined to turn opportunities into lasting outcomes," he said.

The government's "Finance+" approach, Chan pointed out, aims to develop new growth engines, support new industries and finance Hong Kong's green transition.

"Hong Kong brings together capital, innovators, enterprises and professional expertise.

"We want to put these strengths to fuller use, thereby developing new growth engines, supporting new industries, helping businesses transform and expand, as well as financing the green transition.

"The question is not simply how much capital we attract but what that capital makes possible."

Chan noted that Hong Kong's close connection with the mainland is central to this role, helping take technologies from the laboratory to the market at scale while marrying mainland strengths with international capital and global markets.

He cited strong IPO momentum in this regard, saying Hong Kong raised some HK$388 billion in the first nine months of this year, which was more than double that of a year earlier.

International investors from the United States, Europe, Southeast Asia and the Middle East are major players, while enterprises from the last two regions as well as Central Asia are exploring listing or bond-issuance opportunities.

On innovation and technology, Chan said the Northern Metropolis project is more than just about land and buildings.

"We are bringing education, research, talent, enterprises and industry together to create a new engine of growth," he said.

He highlighted the Hetao co-operation zone as a clear example, where Hong Kong and mainland authorities are strengthening cooperation in clinical research and drug regulation, attracting international pharmaceutical companies to conduct research and set up manufacturing facilities.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Samsung profits up a record 780pc despite AI jitters
articles.excerpt: Massive demand for AI chips delivered record quarterly profits to South Korea's Samsung Electronics on Thursday, but shares fell as…
articles.fullText:
Massive demand for AI chips delivered record quarterly profits to South Korea's Samsung Electronics on Thursday, but shares fell as investors questioned the resilience of the global tech boom.

Samsung is the world's largest maker of memory chips – components in short supply as advanced types are snapped up for use in data centres powering artificial intelligence.

The company posted July-September operating profit at 107.4 trillion won (US$80.5 billion) – up more than 780 percent year-on-year.

It marked the first time any technology company had reported quarterly operating profit over 100 trillion won, Samsung said.

Net profit jumped more than 510 percent from last year to 75.1 trillion won, while sales reached 195.3 trillion won.

The global race to build data centres to train and run chatbots, image generators and other AI tools has turbocharged the fortunes of Samsung and other chipmakers, despite concerns that the sector may be overvalued.

Samsung shares fell more than five percent on Thursday morning.

Investors were disappointed by a miss of market expectations for operating profit by the semiconductor division, according to Bloomberg News.

The company's memory business achieved "another record-breaking quarter by managing its product mix, with a focus on AI products, amid capacity constraints," Samsung said in a statement.

"Strong demand momentum for servers led to higher market prices across all applications." (AFP)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Bus-only lanes 'just the ticket to cut Huanggang jams'
articles.excerpt: The chairman of the Non-Franchised Public Bus Association of Hong Kong, Eddie Choi, said on Thursday he believed that dedicated…
articles.fullText:
The chairman of the Non-Franchised Public Bus Association of Hong Kong, Eddie Choi, said on Thursday he believed that dedicated transport lanes at Huanggang checkpoint could effectively reduce traffic congestion during peak hours this weekend.

Authorities announced on Wednesday that priority would be given to public transport to manage vehicular traffic peaks at the crossing between 11pm and 2am on Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

Late-night outbound passenger flow surged last weekend as scores of visitors left the city after attending a concert in Kai Tak and Halloween festivities elsewhere.

"The reason there was traffic congestion last Saturday is because many cars and taxis used the lanes before they reached the control zone," Choi told an RTHK radio programme.

"With the dedicated lanes extended, I think traffic police officers need to be stationed at the scene to prevent cars or taxis at the border crossing from driving onto the lanes and creating traffic congestion on San Tin Highway.

“Improvements also need to be made to the holding area for vehicles waiting to enter the new Huanggang port.”

With proper arrangements made to separate the flow of cars from that of buses, Choi said he believed the journey time for cross-border buses from urban areas to the port could be kept within 40 minutes.

Legislative Council transport panel chairman Ben Chan also welcomed the government's move to give priority to public transport during vehicular traffic peaks at the crossing, saying it gives travellers an extra incentive to take buses.

"I think in Hong Kong the most successful measure is public transport [prioritisation]. This time, the government will arrange more bus lines to service during peak hours, and also the police will facilitate public transport to use the [dedicated lanes] to avoid them from getting trapped on the roads. So I think people will try to use public transport this week," he said.

In a Facebook post, the Transport Department said public transport operators have reserved sufficient vehicles and manpower to cope with the expected travel surge over the weekend.

It said five cross-border bus routes connecting urban areas to Huanggang port will step up their services during late-night periods on Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

Special cross-border buses will also head for Huanggang and Shenzhen Bay ports from Kai Tak after concerts on Friday and Saturday, and passengers are reminded to purchase bus tickets in advance.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Brewers sink Rays for first-ever World Series crown
articles.excerpt: The Milwaukee Brewers won the first World Series title in franchise history on Wednesday, beating the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1…
articles.fullText:
The Milwaukee Brewers won the first World Series title in franchise history on Wednesday, beating the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 to clinch victory in Major League Baseball's championship showcase.

Rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt drove in one run, plated another with a sacrifice fly and scored as the Brewers – denied a sweep by the Rays' thrilling extra-innings comeback win on Tuesday – celebrated a four games to one victory in the best-of-seven series at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Milwaukee's first World Series title comes 44 years after their only other trip to the Fall Classic, when they lost to St. Louis in seven games in 1982.

The Brewers, who swept the defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, gained an early 1-0 edge on Pratt's single to center field that scored Brice Turang in the top of the second inning.

Pratt was cut down trying to reach second base and the Rays escaped the inning without further damage.

Pratt singled again – his sixth hit in six straight at-bats – and scored on David Hamilton's single up the middle as the Brewers doubled their lead in the top of the fifth.

Milwaukee added two more runs for a 4-0 lead in the sixth, when Rays reliever Garrett Cleavinger hit Christian Yelich to open the inning.

William Contreras followed with a double to left field that scored Yelich.

After Turang belted a single Tyler Wells took the mound for Tampa Bay. He struck out Sal Frelick before Pratt lofted a sacrifice fly to right field that allowed Contreras to score.

Milwaukee's flame-throwing pitching ace Jacob Misiorowski, who led the major leagues with 252 strikeouts in the regular season, recorded just two. But he pitched five and two-thirds scoreless innings, giving up just two hits before exiting with apparent leg cramps.

Misiorowski didn't get his first strikeout of the game until the fourth inning.

He then gave up a two-out single to Chandler Simpson, who reached second on a fielding error by Sal Frelick as Liam Hicks – who had reached first when he was hit by a Misiorowski pitch – advanced to third.

Misiorowski escaped the jam when Ben Williamson grounded out to third to strand the Rays runners in scoring position.

Trailing by four runs, the Rays got a glimmer of a chance in the bottom of the seventh when Chandler Simpson's one-out chopper was mis-handled by Brewers catcher Contreras, whose high throw down the right field line allowed Simpson to make it to second base.

Simpson reached third base on Richie Palacios's ground out, but Brewers reliever Abner Uribe retired Victor Mesa Jr. to end the threat.

Simpson drove in the Rays' only run, with a double in the bottom of the ninth, but there would be no miracle comeback and the Rays remain in search of a first title, having now come up empty in three World Series appearances. (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: HKMA warns of interest rate risks as Fed holds steady
articles.excerpt: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on Thursday reminded the public to carefully manage interest rate risks when making property…
articles.fullText:
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on Thursday reminded the public to carefully manage interest rate risks when making property, investment or borrowing decisions, after the US Federal Reserve kept its benchmark rate unchanged.

The Fed's Federal Open Market Committee decided to hold the target range for the federal funds rate at 3.75 to four percent, a move in line with market expectations.

"Hong Kong's monetary and financial markets have continued to operate in an orderly manner," the HKMA said in a statement.

It noted that with the persistent interest rate differential between the Hong Kong and US dollars, trade activities may cause the local currency to gradually ease.

However, the HKMA said the outlook for the Hong Kong dollar and interbank rates could vary depending on factors such as market risk appetite for carry trades and the supply-demand conditions for the local currency, which are in turn influenced by capital market activities and other seasonal factors.

It added that US interest rate adjustments remain subject to considerable uncertainty and will depend on developments in inflation, the labour market and other economic data, which may in turn affect the interest rate environment in Hong Kong.

The HKMA said it will continue to closely monitor market developments to maintain monetary and financial stability.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: HK slips as Korean results raise stakes for AI giants
articles.excerpt: Asian shares gave up earlier gains on Thursday as AI-related earnings announcements prompted wildly mixed responses, raising the stakes for…
articles.fullText:
Asian shares gave up earlier gains on Thursday as AI-related earnings announcements prompted wildly mixed responses, raising the stakes for Amazon and Intel results due later in the day.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index opened down six points, or 0.03 percent, at 23,088.

The tech index slipped 19 points, or 0.5 percent, to 3,834 while the China Enterprises Index inched down six points, or 0.08 percent, to 7,797.

Up north, the Shanghai Composite Index opened down four points, or 0.13 percent, at 3,676.

The Shenzhen Component Index fell 94 points, or 0.82 percent, to 11,379 while the ChiNext Index lost 38 points, or 1.46 percent, to open at 2,596.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei opened 172 points, or 0.27 percent, at 64,126 but regained ground to be 11 points off the pace at one stage before noon.

In Seoul, the Kospi inched up four points, or 0.08 percent, to open at 6,017, gained ground before slipping into loss territory to the tune of 182 points at one stage before lunch.

The opening losses for Asian markets came as a hefty cash burn at Alphabet sent its shares 10 percent lower in after-hours trading, wiping nearly US$400 billion off its market value. That drove Nasdaq futures one percent lower. Microsoft, by contrast, beat forecasts with better-than-expected cash flows that lifted its shares by three percent.

Overnight, the US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady as widely expected, but two committee members voted for a hike. Chairman Kevin Warsh struck a more confident note on the inflation outlook during his press conference, sparking a rally in Treasuries.

However, the bigger test came from earnings. Samsung Electronics said on Thursday its operating profit rose nearly ninefold to a record high in the third quarter, driven by robust demand for AI chips. Its shares still slid more than four percent.

"The reason why Alphabet is down is because their traditional revenue service of ad generation has been impacted by the very thing which is the AI boom. So it's causing a mix of results for Google," said Jamie Hannah, deputy head of investments at VanEck.

"Both of Alphabet and Microsoft confirmed that the AI revenue generation is still solid. We saw that through the data centre growth, the cloud services. So that part of the business is solid, which then flows into a lot of the information coming out of Asia with SK Hynix yesterday as well in Korea." (Reuters & Xinhua)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes
articles.excerpt: US officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against…
articles.fullText:
US officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week’s midterm elections in the United States — as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter.

Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by US diplomats and defence officials.

President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical November 3 elections in the US are over.

Those threats and the fresh US pushes for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon.

The White House and US officials declined to comment.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran “continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed” and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month -- summarily rejected by Trump -- that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a ceasefire.

The United Arab Emirates foreign ministry issued a statement urging the sides to “exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions” and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that began in late February.

The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard -- roughly 9,000 troops in all -- from San Diego to the Persian Gulf to bolster the US military in the region.

The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that's driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy. (AP)

Edited by Altis Wong

articles.title: Alphabet shares plummet after revenue miss
articles.excerpt: Google parent Alphabet on Wednesday missed Wall Street profit and revenue expectations, and AI spending accelerated its cash burn, sending…
articles.fullText:
Google parent Alphabet on Wednesday missed Wall Street profit and revenue expectations, and AI spending accelerated its cash burn, sending its shares down more than 10 percent in extended trading.

Capital expenditures, driven by AI, will increase significantly in 2027, said Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi, adding that this year's capex forecast was unchanged. She said she also expected near-term margin pressure from the use of third-party cloud capacity.

The tech giant reported negative free cash flow of US$9.07 billion, compared with analyst expectations that it would come close to breaking even, according to data compiled by LSEG.

The results reflect the huge costs of the AI buildout, with investors in the sector concerned both by potential overspending and the risk of falling behind rivals by not spending enough.

The quarterly cash burn is an increase from US$5.9 billion in the prior quarter, which was the first time the company went into the negative in its 22-year history as a public company.

Alphabet's cash burn was driven by spending to boost cloud capacity and fund AI research. It reported a US$7.66 billion operating income loss in "Alphabet-level activities," which it said primarily reflected expenses related to AI research and development.

The tech giant's total revenue for the third quarter was US$127.6 billion, short of analysts' estimate of US$128.2 billion, according to LSEG data.

The revenue miss was caused by Google's core advertising business that reported US$82.01 billion in revenue, about US$1.41 billion short of expectations.

Net income available to common shareholders fell 25 percent to US$26.17 billion, and adjusted earnings per share of US$2.67 missed Wall Street targets of US$3.02.

Earlier on Wednesday, Google sought to preempt its results and counter the perception it had fallen behind in the AI race by announcing its new Gemini 4 Carbon model, which CEO Sundar Pichai told analysts during the earnings call meant it was again "leading at the frontier."

Revenue at Google Cloud exceeded estimates and more than doubled to US$30.71 billion in the third quarter ended September 30, but was not enough to make up for the ad-side performance. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: China leverages Taiwan’s reverence for Sun Yat-sen to promote ‘reunification’
articles.excerpt: Shared history fosters cross-strait kinship, but analysts say China’s framing sways only those already pro-Beijing.
articles.fullText:
Beijing is trying to use national hero Sun Yat-sen – who is also revered in Taiwan – to frame “reunification” with the democratic island as the fulfillment of a common national destiny, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
Ahead of the 160th anniversary of Sun’s birth on Nov. 12, the mainland has planned official commemorations, and Taiwan’s government warned that Beijing was using the revolutionary leader’s legacy to further an “ anti-independence, pro-reunification ” strategy.
Taiwan considers Sun to be the “father of the country.” He helped lead the revolution that ended China’s imperial system and became the Republic of China’s first provisional president in 1912. The government of the Republic of China fled to Taiwan in 1949 when Chiang Kai-shek’s nationalists lost the Chinese Civil War to Mao Zedong’s communists. Taiwan still uses “Republic of China” as its official name.
In Beijing’s view, Sun is the “forerunner of the revolution.” Mao is considered to have continued in his footsteps, and the communist “People’s Republic of China” is said to be the realization of Sun’s unfinished vision. It is this version of history that China wants to push, Jozef Huljak, a political science doctoral candidate at Constantine the Philosopher University in Slovakia whose research examines Taiwan’s cultural and public diplomacy, told RFA.
“In my view, Beijing’s core strategy is a battle over words: if the world accepts its version of history, a takeover can be sold as ‘reunification,’” Huljak said.
Soldiers stand in front of a Taiwan flag and a portrait of Sun Yat-sen, the founding father of the Republic of China, after Taiwan’s military demonstrated combat readiness ahead of the upcoming Lunar New Year holidays in an annual exercise in Hsinchu, Taiwan, Jan. 7, 2025.
(Ann Wang/Reuters) Though China’s communist government has never governed Taiwan, it considers the democratic island to be a rogue province. It claims the island as its territory and has not renounced using force to bring it under Beijing’s control.
In addition to diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan, China’s historical messaging promotes a national belonging intended to make political union appear both legitimate and inevitable.
China’s own policy documents describe history and culture as forces driving unification. A 2022 white paper on Taiwan presented national unity as a longstanding Chinese aspiration and tied its achievement to the country’s national rejuvenation.
Sun as a political tool
Sun’s connection to China’s Taiwan policy is explicit. Beijing organized the cross-strait Sun Yat-sen Forum in his ancestral birthplace in June, and about 1,300 Taiwanese participants attended.
At that event, Pan Xianzhang, a deputy head of China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, urged people on both sides to draw inspiration from Sun while adhering to the “one-China principle,” Beijing’s doctrine that asserts Taiwan is an inalienable part of China.
“Beijing’s use of Sun works because Taipei still props him up,” Huljak said.
But the same historical figure can carry different political meanings. During an April visit to Sun’s mausoleum in Nanjing, Cheng Li-wun, chairperson of Taiwan’s main opposition Kuomintang, or KMT, – the Nationalist party founded by Sun – invoked his legacy to advocate reconciliation and dialogue. She also pointed to Taiwan’s democratic development as an expression of his founding principles.
Cheng Li-wun, chairperson of the Kuomintang, Taiwan's largest opposition party, speaks upon visiting Sun Yat-sen's Mausoleum in Nanjing, China April 8, 2026.
(via REUTERS) The KMT’s own account of the visit emphasized the continuation of Sun’s ideals in Taiwan and the promotion of peaceful cross-strait relations.
A broader repertoire
Sun’s birth anniversary is part of a wider pattern in which Chinese authorities connect history to a shared national identity and political unity with Taiwan.
Another figure honored on both sides of the strait is Zheng Chenggong, also known as Koxinga, who expelled the Dutch from Taiwan in 1662 and established a regime there. Beijing describes him as a national hero who recovered Chinese territory.
But in Taiwan the way Zheng is remembered depends on who you ask. For some, he is seen as analogous to Chiang Kai-shek, as both were military leaders who lost their respective campaigns on the mainland, fled to Taiwan, and vowed to return. To others, he is seen as having established a kingdom on Taiwan independent from mainland control.
The Portrait of Koxinga—a mid-17th century hanging scroll exhibited in the National Palace Museum in Taiwan
(National Palace Museum via Wikimedia Commons) In September 2024, China’s Taiwan Affairs Office highlighted commemorations marking the 400th anniversary of Zheng’s birth alongside exhibitions about families separated by the Taiwan Strait.
The two sides also frame the end of World War II differently.
In October 2025, China’s legislature designated Oct. 25 as a day commemorating what it calls Taiwan’s recovery from Japanese rule in 1945. The decision described that event as an important link in the historical and legal basis for Taiwan belonging to China.
But in Taiwan’s view, it was the Republic of China authorities who took over Taiwan’s administration after Japan’s surrender in 1945. The People’s Republic of China was founded four years later and has never ruled Taiwan.
Huljak said these competing interpretations of history and historical figures matter internationally as well as within Taiwan. In his assessment, acceptance of Beijing’s historical vocabulary can help normalize its present-day claims among foreign audiences unfamiliar with the distinction.
Symbols and their limits
The challenge for Beijing is that Taiwan’s identity has diverged since the Chinese civil war, the analysts said.
Under Chiang Kai-shek, the KMT claimed to represent all of China and ruled Taiwan through an authoritarian system. Martial law ended in 1987, and the island held its first direct presidential election in 1996, establishing a democratic basis for political authority.
President Chiang Kai-shek of Nationalist China delivers an address at a city hall reception in Taipei, March 2, 1950.
(Spencer Mosa/AP) That transformation helps explain the gap analysts see between Sun Yat-sen’s institutional prominence and his emotional relevance to many people in Taiwan.
“Claiming to be the true inheritor of Sun’s legacy is one of many similar methods Beijing uses to court Taiwanese and try to forge common bonds, but these claims have limited currency among a people for whom Sun has limited emotional resonance,” Sasha B. Chhabra, a Taiwan-based security analyst and publisher of the Formosa Review newsletter, told RFA.
Chhabra said Sun remained particularly important to KMT supporters in Taiwan, who prefer engagement with the mainland over independence. Huljak also identified KMT supporters and potential swing voters as audiences Beijing hoped to reach.
Neither assessment, however, establishes that commemorations change political preferences. Shared respect for a historical figure can provide an opening for contact without producing agreement over sovereignty or support for Communist rule.
For Chhabra, figures associated with Taiwan’s own political development have greater relevance to many residents than the revolutionary founder honored by both governments.
“Taiwanese are more interested in commemorating figures with a tangible legacy in the country, such as presidents Lee Teng-hui or Chiang Jing-kuo,” he said, referring to Taiwan’s first directly elected president and his predecessor, who lifted martial law in 1987.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: UK budget lifts bank tax to offset energy bills
articles.excerpt: Britain's Labour government will increase a tax on profits earned by banks to help reduce soaring energy bills for millions…
articles.fullText:
Britain's Labour government will increase a tax on profits earned by banks to help reduce soaring energy bills for millions of UK households, finance minister John Healey announced in his budget on Wednesday.

The first budget of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's administration was delivered to parliament against a harsh global backdrop of rising inflation and borrowing costs, and the fallout of the Iran war.

Despite the constraints, Healey pledged to raise UK defence spending to three percent of gross domestic product by 2030 – a commitment he had pushed for before resigning as defence secretary over insufficient military funding under previous PM Keir Starmer.

Britain's economy will grow slightly faster than forecast this year – by 1.2 percent – before slowing to a worse-than-expected 1.0 percent in 2027 – driven by effects of the war in the Middle East, Healey said as he delivered the government's annual budget.

"Fiscal discipline is my first commitment," he added, in comments welcomed by bond markets as UK yields dipped Wednesday.

Healey, whose official title is Chancellor of the Exchequer, promised "immediate" support for households and businesses in the face of "global economic storms".

Labour is to double to six percent a surcharge on profits earned by banks operating in the UK.

Lasting for 15 months from January, the tax increase will raise £1.5 billion, Britain's fiscal watchdog, the Office for Budget Responsibility, said in an accompanying statement.

"This is net of an estimated £190 million reduction in receipts as some banks are assumed to move profits out of the UK in response to the higher tax rate," the OBR said.

Banks had expected to be hit harder, resulting in share prices of most UK lenders, including Barclays and NatWest, rising.

Oil and gas giants operating in the UK, which are enjoying bumper profits thanks to the US-Iran war, are already subject to a windfall tax.

Healey said a direct payment of £100 will be sent to 20 million households, as gas and electricity prices surge in large part owing to the Middle East conflict.

Further measures to lower energy bills included removing fixed fees on gas bills and extending a freeze on fuel duty.

Healey's budget plans were constrained by his commitment to abide by predecessor Rachel Reeves's fiscal rules, stating that day-to-day outlay must balance with state tax receipts.

In the runup to the budget, UK media reports suggested government spending cuts could occur next year.

Responding to the budget, the leader of the main opposition Conservatives Kemi Badenoch said: "We all know why he's delayed until tomorrow, difficult (budget) decisions he should have taken today.

"It is because the prime minister wants to keep the option of an early general election, putting his party's interests before the country's."

Since Burnham replaced Starmer as prime minister in July, Labour's support has risen among voters in opinion polls.

Following Badenoch's comments, Burnham again ruled out the prospect of a snap general election in the next year, adding the budget had taken "a very prudent and stable approach". (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Microsoft beats cloud revenue, sales estimates
articles.excerpt: Microsoft on Wednesday forecast fiscal second-quarter cloud growth and overall sales that beat Wall Street estimates, sending shares up more…
articles.fullText:
Microsoft on Wednesday forecast fiscal second-quarter cloud growth and overall sales that beat Wall Street estimates, sending shares up more than 5 percent in after-hours trading.

The forecast came after Microsoft had earlier beaten expectations for first-quarter cloud revenue, offering fresh evidence that its hefty AI investments were paying off as Wall Street grows increasingly wary of Big Tech's debt-fuelled spending.

The software and cloud company also generated US$18.6 billion in free cash flow in its fiscal first quarter ended September – some US$10 billion more than analysts expected – as capital spending came in below the company's own forecast and Microsoft's Azure cloud computing business surged 48 percent.

Microsoft said it expects second-quarter Azure growth of 49 to 50 percent, above analyst estimates of 47.6 percent, according to Visible Alpha data. The company forecast overall sales of US$96 billion to US$97.1 billion, above estimates of US$95.6 billion, according to LSEG data.

That financial firepower set Microsoft apart from rivals such as Alphabet and Meta, whose heavy AI investments have squeezed free cash flow and increased their reliance on borrowing. Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of US$9.07 billion in the third quarter as capital spending jumped, overshadowing a doubling of its cloud sales and sending its shares down 8 percent in extended trading.

Microsoft shares have risen about 9 percent so far this year, through Wednesday's close. Its five-year credit default swaps – a measure of perceived default risk – remain the tightest among the largest tech companies, according to Truist, even as spreads have widened across much of the AI trade.

The results also show Microsoft capitalising on corporate demand for AI, easing fears that the technology threatens its software empire and that its AI fortunes are too closely tied to unprofitable OpenAI.

CEO Satya Nadella has sought to capture that demand by giving customers cheaper options, as businesses grapple with the rising cost of deploying AI. Microsoft has rolled out a string of lower-cost models, while its new Copilot Cowork agent allows users to switch between models.

"By helping organisations build and own their own intelligence, and earning trust through agent safety and security, we are translating our innovation into growing adoption," Nadella said in a statement on Wednesday.

"Microsoft's first-quarter report was about as clean as it gets for a company this size," said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com. "After Meta's and Alphabet's numbers revived AI-spending anxiety, this is the counterweight. Demand still exceeds supply, the commercial backlog is enormous, and returns are finally showing up in earnings and overall revenue."

Revenue at Microsoft's Azure cloud computing business grew to US$33.17 billion in the quarter, topping Visible Alpha's estimate of US$32.84 billion. Overall revenue rose by a fifth to US$92.28 billion, and an adjusted profit of US$4.89 per share beat an average estimate of US$4.73 a share. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: City, Liverpool scrape into League Cup quarter-finals
articles.excerpt: Liverpool beat Chelsea in a dramatic penalty shoot-out to reach the League Cup quarter-finals, while holders Manchester City survived a…
articles.fullText:
Liverpool beat Chelsea in a dramatic penalty shoot-out to reach the League Cup quarter-finals, while holders Manchester City survived a scare against Brighton on Wednesday.

In a clash between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso, it was the Liverpool manager who took the bragging rights in the last-16 tie at Anfield.

A 1-1 draw in normal time set the stage for the shoot-out as Chelsea's Morgan Rogers netted from the spot, only for Cody Gakpo to equalise with a penalty of his own just before half-time.

Chelsea's Valentin Barco hit the post in the shoot-out before Liverpool's Kostas Tsimikas wasted a chance to win it when he blazed over.

Ryan Gravenberch was denied by Chelsea keeper Mike Penders, but Giorgi Mamardashvili saved Emmanuel Emegha's kick to keep Liverpool alive.

After Joe Gomez scored for Liverpool, Blues defender Wesley Fofana miscued into the Kop as the hosts advanced.

It was former Liverpool midfielder Alonso's third defeat in his three visits to Anfield as a manager following losses with Bayer Leverkusen in 2024 and Real Madrid in 2025.

In their debut campaigns at Liverpool, Jurgen Klopp and Arne Slot both reached the League Cup final and Iraola is on course to follow in their footsteps with the 10-time winners of the competition.

Alonso made just four changes to the Chelsea side that lost 2-0 at home to Tottenham on Saturday, while Iraola made seven changes from Liverpool's 2-0 win against Brighton on Sunday.

Rogers put Chelsea in front with a 40th-minute penalty after Gravenberch clattered into Moises Caicedo.

But Liverpool were level three minutes later with a penalty of their own as Gakpo converted from the spot following Fofana's handball.

At the Etihad Stadium, City were pushed to the brink by Brighton in a 2-2 draw before winning on penalties.

City boss Enzo Maresca made nine changes after Saturday's loss at Aston Villa, which ended the leaders' 100 percent start to the Premier League campaign.

Erling Haaland, Ruben Dias, Elliot Anderson and Gianluigi Donnarumma were among the City stars rested.

Brighton went in front after 30 minutes when Malick Yalcouye steered Georginio Rutter's shot past Geronimo Rulli from five yards.

Mateo Kovacic hauled City level 20 minutes later with a fine finish that curled into the far corner from 25 yards.

Rutter restored Brighton's lead two minutes after half-time, slotting home from Jaouen Hadjam's cut-back.

Vitor Reis deflected in Rayan Cherki's 72nd-minute free-kick to equalise for City.

Kovacic's penalty was saved by Jason Steele in the shoot-out, but Rulli denied Brighton's Yasin Ayari and Lewis Dunk to send City into the last eight.

The sides meet again in the Premier League at the Etihad on Saturday.

Bournemouth extended their blistering run with a 3-0 win against Aston Villa at the Vitality Stadium.

The Cherries beat AC Milan 3-0 in the Europa League last week and followed that up with a 3-0 win at Manchester United in the Premier League on Sunday.

Marco Rose's men dispatched Villa in equally emphatic fashion as goals from Amine Adli, Lewis Cook and Alvaro Rodriguez made it five successive wins in all competitions.

Crystal Palace eased the pressure on under-fire boss Pierre Sage with a 1-0 win at Fulham.

Eddie Nketiah struck in the 37th minute to give struggling Palace their first win in five games in all competitions.

Sunderland enjoyed a welcome respite from their Premier League struggles with a 3-2 victory against Brentford at the Stadium of Light.

Sitting bottom of the Premier League, Sunderland swatted aside the Bees with goals from Chemsdine Talbi, Tymur Tutierov and Malick Fofana.

Callum Wilson and Igor Thiago netted too late to save Brentford.

Fourth-tier Fleetwood reached the quarter-finals with a stunning penalty shoot-out victory over Premier League champions Arsenal on Tuesday.

Everton host Newcastle in the last game of the fourth round on Thursday. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: US stocks eye big tech earnings as Fed holds rates
articles.excerpt: Wall Street stocks finished higher on Wednesday after a choppy session, digesting a status quo US Federal Reserve decision as…
articles.fullText:
Wall Street stocks finished higher on Wednesday after a choppy session, digesting a status quo US Federal Reserve decision as markets monitored the latest earnings from US tech giants.

The Fed, as expected, held interest rates steady, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation despite persistently elevated pricing pressure. Two dissenting members of the panel voted for an immediate interest rate increase.

Major US indices spent most of the day in positive territory but traded within a fairly narrow range. The broad-based S&P 500 finished up 0.3 percent.

Art Hogan of B Riley Wealth Management said the market's biggest priority this week is sifting through a deluge of earnings, including Microsoft and Google parent Alphabet, two of the biggest companies in artificial intelligence.

The tech results are "100 percent the focus," said Hogan. "The market is taking a 'nothing to see here' attitude towards what the Fed did today."

Citing higher energy prices in recent weeks, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said "our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy," Warsh said at a news conference.

Still, he said the Fed needed more information in the coming weeks to "determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the two-percent goal."

The AI trade enjoyed a broad lift earlier on Wednesday from blockbuster earnings from the South Korean chip giant SK hynix, which soared almost 11 percent, helping to lift Seoul's Kospi index more than six percent.

SK hynix, a specialist supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips to US industry behemoth Nvidia, unveiled plans to return an additional US$45 billion to shareholders after reporting operating profits about seven times the year-ago level.

The global race to build AI data centres has transformed the company's fortunes, despite concerns that the sector may be overvalued.

The report by SK hynix added to optimism surrounding the sector after Anthropic, the creator of Claude AI, said on Monday that its first-half revenue surged about 1,300 percent and flagged heavy capital spending ahead, fuelling enthusiasm ahead of an expected IPO next month.

AI stocks took a beating earlier this month over worries about the massive investments and debt levels in the sector, but then welcomed Anthropic's IPO.

In other markets, oil prices moved higher following reports that the United States is planning to mount a new military attack in Iran after the US midterm elections.

Gains in the US dollar, meanwhile, moderated after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference.

Warsh is saying the Fed's first interest rate hike in September "had a large impact, which indicates that he doesn't think the Fed has that much more to do," said Adam Button, currency analyst at investingLive.

The S&P 500 rose 0.3 percent, to 7,744, the Dow rose 0.2 percent, to 52,475, while the Nasdaq rose 0.3 percent, to 26,550. (AFP)

Edited by Robert Kemp

articles.title: US Federal Reserve holds rates steady, as expected
articles.excerpt: The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs…
articles.fullText:
The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week's US midterm elections while it awaits further data on inflation, which the central bank said "remains elevated."

The 10-2 decision to maintain the Fed's benchmark interest rate within the 3.75-4 percent range came with an upgraded assessment of an economy that the central bank now says is growing at a "strong pace." Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh also expressed confidence that inflation can be lowered to the 2 percent target without having to "throw sand in the gears" and slow growth or raise unemployment.

Warsh, speaking at a press conference after the end of a two-day policy meeting, said he expects a report on third-quarter gross domestic product on Thursday to show strong investment and consumer spending and an acceleration of growth from the first half of the year. Warsh, however, said he still does not think the economy is "too hot" or generating demand-side inflation that needs to be curbed.

"The economy is pointing in the right direction. Is the economy running too hot? Is the economy running too strong? That isn't the judgement of most of my colleagues," said Warsh, arguing, as he has before, that changes in productivity, even pre-dating the artificial intelligence boom, may allow the US to grow faster without as much inflation.

"The goal, in my view... isn't to throw sand in the gears of the economy and throw people out of work. I don't think we have to do that."

Rather, he said, a higher Fed policy rate is already showing its impact in slightly tighter credit conditions that could, for example, slow business investment and which arguably contributed to recent stock market declines, another potential source of "disinflation" if it slows spending among wealthier families.

In comments to CNBC on Thursday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the administration continues to have faith that Warsh will "find the right balance" between the 2 percent inflation goal and continuing economic growth.

The rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee's latest policy statement, however, hinted that more rate hikes may be needed, and some of Warsh's colleagues have been explicit in their concerns that demand, fuelled by AI and healthy consumer spending, is starting to drive prices higher.

Between now and the next policy meeting in December, "the accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal," the FOMC said. "The Committee will deliver price stability."

Fed Governor Lisa Cook, currently being targeted by President Donald Trump for removal from the central bank, cast her first dissent on a central bank policy decision on Wednesday, favouring a quarter-percentage-point rate hike. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, a consistently hawkish voice, also dissented in favour of a rate increase.

Market reaction was muted, with US stocks paring gains slightly after the decision but ending higher on the day. Longer-dated US Treasury yields extended their rise. Short-term interest-rate futures rose a bit, as traders scaled back a bit on bets of Fed rate hikes ahead.

"The forces keeping the Federal Reserve hawkish haven't faded. Diesel and gasoline prices remain elevated, AI-driven inflation isn't easing, and the labour market remains resilient," said Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics.

The outcome of this week's meeting was widely expected after top Fed officials indicated they saw no rush to raise rates again following the quarter-percentage-point increase approved last month, despite inflation data in the meantime that was stronger than forecast and concerns that price pressures are broadening across the economy.

Financial markets are still pricing in a couple of additional rate hikes in the coming months, though with slightly less conviction than before Warsh spoke on Wednesday. Pricing shows about an 80 percent chance of a rate hike at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting, with another increase in borrowing costs likely by March. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
articles.excerpt: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms…
articles.fullText:
Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments.

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT

An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.

Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes.

“There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.”

The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says.

Download the report

This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

articles.title: Wang Fuk Court fire report released
articles.excerpt: (To watch the full press conference with sign language interpretation, click here .) Chief Executive John Lee today announced that…
articles.fullText:
(To watch the full press conference with sign language interpretation, click here .)

Chief Executive John Lee today announced that the Government will launch comprehensive reforms following the release of the independent committee’s report on the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po.

The blaze resulted in the deaths of 168 people, including a fireman who died in the line of duty. At a press conference unveiling the report, Mr Lee and principal officials bowed in apology for the pain and sorrow caused to the affected families and the community.

Addressing political accountability, Mr Lee announced that Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho had tendered her resignation. He has made a submission to the Central People's Government, recommending her removal from the post.

“Considering that the fire took place in Wang Fuk Court and it falls within the purview of the Independent Checking Unit, which is under the Housing Bureau, the Secretary for Housing should take political accountability.

“I also set two requirements for my political team. First, continue in their respective positions to exert the utmost efforts amidst the reforms and the substantial amount of work ahead.

“Second, learn from the incident, strengthen leadership and pursue more vigorously result-oriented governance,” he said.

With effect from today, Ms Ho's duties as the Secretary for Housing are suspended. Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong has concurrently assumed the post of Acting Secretary for Housing.

The Government received the independent committee’s report last Thursday. After seeking legal advice, parts of the report have been redacted to prevent any actual or perceived undue prejudice to ongoing criminal prosecutions.

The report highlighted that the rapid spread of the fire and the high number of casualties were caused by the suspected substitution of fire-retardant scaffolding nets with non-fire-retardant ones, the use of non-fire-retardant foam boards and other flammable materials during the works, as well as the creation of access openings in the escape staircases for convenience.

It also pointed out that the long-standing regulatory system for building maintenance and renovation relies heavily on the integrity and professional conduct of industry professionals and contractors. However, certain individuals are suspected of abandoning their supervisory and management responsibilities, rendering oversight effectively non-existent.

Deficiencies and failings were detailed across relevant government departments, including the Independent Checking Unit under the Housing Bureau, the Buildings Department, the Fire Services Department and the Labour Department.

Furthermore, the report noted that because building maintenance and renovation projects involve substantial sums of money, they have become targets for triads and criminals. These groups have formed syndicates to rig bids and monopolise the market through intimidation, fraud and corruption.

The independent committee put forward 120 recommendations in its report, which has been published online for public viewing.

Noting that bid-rigging is the root cause of the problems, that the Mandatory Building Inspection Scheme has deficiencies, and that property owners lack the professional knowledge to protect themselves from fraud, Mr Lee said the Government will implement comprehensive and systemic reform .

The Government will legislate against bid-rigging in building maintenance and renovation projects, establish a cross-departmental task force to combat relevant crimes, and set up a Building Maintenance Support & Services Council.
