On Sept. 1, 2026 the Golog Education Department officially opened the newly established Golog Tsoshar Middle School in eastern Qinghai. According to Chinese state media, the school enrolled 1,200 students, including 1,090 Tibetans, many from farming and nomadic families.
Authorities have described the relocation of students from Golog to the lower-lying Tsoshar area as part of an effort to expand residential education in the highlands. It remains unclear whether students from Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School were transferred to the new institution.
Golog Ziling (Xining) Middle School, a state-run boarding school in Xining, was also opened on Sept. 1, 2019. According to official figures for 2024, it had 800 students, including 778 Tibetans, all from Golog. The school’s official introduction identifies fostering a shared sense of community among the Chinese nation as a central goal of its education.
In September 2026, the Golog prefecture government also launched a public language promotion week encouraging students to learn and use standard Chinese and emphasizing unity among the Chinese people.
Earlier school closures
The latest shutdowns follow several other closures of Tibetan educational institutions in Golog in recent years.
In July 2024, authorities closed Gangjong Sherig Norling School in Machen County after 30 years of operation. Founded by Jigme Gyaltsen in 1994, the institution had about 1,400 students and 58 teachers and staff.
The vocational school combined modern education with instruction in Tibetan language, culture, philosophy and religion. Reports in April 2025 indicated that authorities had permitted it to reopen as a vocational institution, although its curriculum was expected to change.
Dorjeten National Vocational School in Chikdril County (in Golog) was shut down on Dec. 12, 2025, affecting more than 1,300 students, according to reports. Hungkar Dorje Vocational Secondary School in Golog was also closed on June 24, 2026.
The latest closures have raised further questions about the future of Tibetan-language education in the region and whether students from the affected schools will continue to have opportunities to learn their language and cultural traditions.
Background: The three schools
Gangjong Grassland Girls’ School
Founded in 2005 by Tibetan educator Jigme Gyaltsen in Ragya Township, the school was established to provide education for girls, including those from nomadic communities. When it officially opened on Oct. 15, 2005, it had 203 students and 15 teachers. Its curriculum included Tibetan, Chinese and English, as well as mathematics, science, culture and sports.
Gyaltsen described his educational philosophy as follows: “The education of girls is the education of mothers, and the education of mothers is the foundation of human education.”
Jasag Village Primary School
Established in 1995 with funds raised by local nomadic families through the former Jasag Village Committee, the school served children from the surrounding community. It was renamed Ragya Township Residential School No. 2 in 2008 and closed in September 2026.
Golog Tadra Orphan School
Founded in 2005 by the late Dr. Tawo Lobsang Palden and his wife, Choenyi Lhamo, the school provided education, accommodation, food, clothing and health care to Tibetan orphans and disadvantaged children. Over two decades, it served thousands of children. Lhamo now lives in Germany.
Translated by Tenzin Dickyi and edited by Tawang for RFA Tibetan

articles.title: China’s sanctions on Taiwan allies project its power, but with limited effect
articles.excerpt: Beijing sent a message by sanctioning officials from Paraguay and Belize, but both remain loyal to Taipei.
articles.fullText:
China’s sanctions against foreign officials over their ties with Taiwan help Beijing project power and warn other governments, even as their financial impact and success in curbing engagement remain limited, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
Beijing imposed sanctions on Oct. 12 against Paraguay’s information and communication technologies minister, Gustavo Villate, and Belize’s foreign minister, Francis Fonseca. Both countries maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan rather than China.
China claims Taiwan is an integral part of its territory and considers it a rogue province. Beijing has sought to persuade governments to switch recognition from Taiwan to China, reducing Taiwan’s network of embassies and official government-to-government relationships.
The Chinese government has described the sanctions as a “warning and deterrence.”
The national flags of Paraguay and Taiwan flutter outside the building housing Taiwan's embassy, in Asuncion, Paraguay, Feb. 25, 2026.
(Cesar Olmedo/Reuters) When China sanctions individuals they don’t quite have the same effect as U.S. or European sanctions, Ed Moon, an independent cross-Strait analyst and founder of intelligence site Strait Signal, told RFA.
“Chinese sanctions are unlikely to have significant impacts on people without major interests in the Chinese banking system, shareholdings or business interests,” he said.
But the penalties serve a purpose beyond imposing financial losses, said Moon. They signal to observers in China and abroad that Beijing can enforce restrictions when it believes its interests have been harmed, and can serve as a warning to countries closely connected to the Chinese economy about dealings with sanctioned individuals.
While sanctions could discourage engagement with Taiwan, there is little evidence that the strategy is causing isolation for Taipei, William Yang, a Northeast Asia analyst at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group, told RFA.
“We haven’t really seen a substantial level of retreat in terms of foreign parliamentarians’ trips to Taiwan or foreign governments’ cooperation with Taiwan,” Yang said.
The assessments point to a distinction between two types of sanctions: those that impose measurable costs and those whose principal effect is to publicize Beijing’s opposition to Taiwan’s international relationships.
Isolating Taiwan
Only 12 countries retain formal diplomatic relations with Taipei. Taiwan also maintains extensive unofficial relationships with countries that recognize Beijing. Those ties include trade, investment and parliamentary exchanges, explaining why China’s penalties have targeted politicians beyond Taiwan’s formal diplomatic allies.
Yang said Beijing’s campaign is meant to show Taiwan’s government and people that it has the power to restrict international engagement with Taipei, while simultaneously showing foreign governments that there will be consequences for treating Taiwan as a sovereign state.
He added Beijing believes its economic influence gives it leverage to intimidate politicians and governments considering closer engagement with Taipei.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said during an Oct. 12 press briefing that the ministers from Paraguay and Belize were sanctioned for supporting Taiwan independence through their contacts with Taipei and spreading false allegations about Chinese cyberattacks.
Belize's Prime Minister Johnny Briceno, left, meets with Taiwan's Vice President Lai Ching-te in Honduras, Jan. 27, 2022.
(Taiwan Presidential Office/AP) The next day, Taiwan’s Premier Cho Jung-tai said that Beijing had no right to interfere in Taiwan’s internal affairs or influence its foreign relations. He said Taiwan would continue working with its allies and other democratic governments to defend freedom and democracy and maintain regional peace and security.
Paraguay and Belize also rejected the sanctions. Paraguay’s Foreign Ministry reaffirmed its support for Taiwan, while Belize said the penalties would not alter its foreign policy and defended its relationship with Taipei as a sovereign decision.
Their cooperation involves more than diplomatic recognition. Paraguayan President Santiago Peña visited Taiwan in May, signing agreements covering cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and computing investment, among other areas. Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung visited Belize in September to deepen bilateral ties.
Do Chinese sanctions work?
Previous cases of Chinese sanctions show the difficulty of turning personal penalties into lasting restrictions on engagement.
In June, China confirmed entry restrictions against New Zealand lawmakers following their visit to Taiwan. Beijing said their trip interfered in China’s internal affairs.
From right to left, Taiwan's Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim, speaking with New Zealand lawmakers Maureen Pugh, Duncan Webb, Laura McClure and David Wilson at the Presidential Office in Taipei, May 7, 2026.
(Presidential Office of Taiwan/AFP) In August 2022, China sanctioned Lithuania’s deputy transport minister, Agnė Vaiciukevičiūtė, after she visited Taiwan. Beijing also suspended exchanges with Vilnius’ transport ministry and paused certain international transportation agreements between the two countries.
That action formed part of a wider dispute after Lithuania allowed a Taiwanese representative office to open in the country in 2021. China downgraded diplomatic relations over the decision.
Cooperation with Taiwan nevertheless continued. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry reported discussions in April 2026 on strengthening economic and technological ties.
The broader outcome is more complicated. Lithuania’s prime minister described the original representative-office decision as a mistake in February as the country sought to repair relations with Beijing.
Because the dispute involved broader diplomatic and economic pressure, analysts say it is difficult to isolate the impact of sanctions against a single official.
Moon said the same difficulty applied to Paraguay and Belize – Beijing has used various public and private forms of pressure for years, so any subsequent policy change could not automatically be attributed to the latest sanctions.
He said changes in diplomatic language, visits and, at the most dramatic end, diplomatic recognition would provide indicators of whether the relationships were shifting.
Past sanctions have also produced backlash.
In March 2021, Beijing sanctioned European lawmakers and institutions in retaliation for European Union sanctions over human rights abuses in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. Although the dispute concerned human rights rather than Taiwan, it similarly targeted individual politicians and their institutions.
The European Parliament responded by freezing consideration of an EU-China investment agreement while the Chinese sanctions remained in place. Beijing lifted the sanctions affecting the EU Parliament’s members and committees in 2025.
Moon said sanctions could carry greater economic weight when directed at people or companies with business interests in China, including in Taiwan.
In a separate action on Oct. 14, Beijing announced restrictions against VWAY, a company linked to the father of Taiwanese legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen.
Pedestrians walk past a giant campaign billboard featuring the Democratic Progressive Party's Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen in Taipei on Oct. 15, 2026.
(I-Hwa Cheng/AFP) China’s Taiwan Affairs Office accused Shen’s father of using VWAY to continue trading with Chinese firms after sanctions were placed on another of his businesses.
Moon cautioned that Taiwan-related business sanctions were not directly comparable with penalties against foreign governments’ officials, given Beijing’s position that Taiwan is part of China.
Yang said the sanctions’ limited results so far did not rule out a stronger deterrent effect in the future. Responses by Taiwan’s remaining diplomatic allies, including whether they protested collectively or moved toward recognizing Beijing, would be important to watch, he said.
“So far it seems like at least the government of Paraguay and Belize are holding their lines,” said Yang.
Beijing could still regard the publicity itself as a result, reinforcing its claims over Taiwan and demonstrating that engagement with Taipei carried consequences, Moon said.
“But I think for Beijing the mere fact it has created a news cycle out of the sanctions will mean it has achieved the desired effect of reinforcing its claims over Taiwan and showing there are consequences, however limited, to siding with Taipei.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: ‘I hope that she will be free before long’ Aung San Suu Kyi’s son Kim Aris says
articles.excerpt: Kim Aris talks to RFA after his first direct contact in 5 years with his mother, under house arrest in…
articles.fullText:
Myanmar’s military-backed government announced on Thursday that former leader Aung San Suu Kyi – currently under house arrest – was allowed to talk for 20 minutes to her son Kim Aris at 2:30 p.m. via a call placed to the Myanmar embassy in London, where Aris resides.
He speaks in an exclusive interview with Radio Free Asia.
Radio Free Asia: After more than five years without direct contact, how did you get the opportunity to speak with your mother and how did the Myanmar Embassy in London reach out to you? How was the call arranged?
Kim Aris: I was informed through the British Foreign Office here that the call may take place. This was last week. And then earlier this week, they confirmed that it would take place, and they accompanied me to the Burmese Embassy this morning.
RFA: During your conversation, did Daw Aung San Suu Kyi mention anything about her health or her daily life?
Kim Aris: Well, she was more concerned about my health and the rest of the family than anything else. But obviously, I asked after her health and how things were, where she is. She wasn’t able to reveal too much, but I know that she’s been held in some residence, I believe in Naypyidaw, and she sounds healthy. But at the same time, I know that she is in some pain because her hand is not very well; she has tendonitis. So at times, the pain is quite extreme, and I think she is even unable to use that hand at times. Nothing too clear. I know that she’s getting a regular six-monthly checkup, but I know that will be a military doctor, so it’s not like having her own personal doctor.
RFA: Do you know whether she has any access to news from the outside world?
Kim Aris: I don’t think she does. As far as I’m aware, she has no radio or television and doesn’t get any newspapers or anything like that. We know that the conversation will have been monitored and recorded, so we can’t talk about anything sensitive. Besides which, there was a lot to talk about just talking about what’s happened in the family over the last five years. So that’s what we talked about.
RFA: During these recent developments , do you believe there could be a political breakthrough on the horizon?
Kim Aris: I sincerely hope so. I think everybody is tired of the fighting now, and people are starting to think that they need to start talking to each other. But I think the first thing that needs to happen before anybody will start talking is the political prisoners, including may may (Burmese expression for “mom”), need to be freed.
RFA: Some observers believe the Myanmar authorities may be looking for a way out of Myanmar’s ongoing political crisis. What is your take on this?
Kim Aris: Well, it’s very clear the military have been trying to be more appealing to the international community, especially following their elections at the end of last year and the beginning of this year. So they are doing whatever they can to try and get people to work with them again. But people need to remember that the military haven’t actually abided by any of what they have said they will have done over the last five years. They have not met the five-point consensus, and yet people are starting to re-engage with them without having seen any evidence of actual progress.
RFA: The Myanmar military authorities have recently been releasing more information about Daw Aung San Suu Kyi. Do you see this as a reason for optimism? What do you think the Myanmar military’s move might be?
Kim Aris: I always have hope, and I do hope that this will result in actual progress and that she will be free before long. And even before she’s free, I want more regular contact with her, and I want to know that she’s receiving external medical treatment.
RFA: Did they promise you could speak with Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, your mother, regularly?
Kim Aris: No, I haven’t heard anything more on that yet.
RFA: You made it very clear that your mother should never be used as a bargaining chip for diplomatic recognition, sanctions relief, or political advantage. You also urged the UK government and others not to trade humanitarian rights for political legitimacy. And now, one of our RFA audience members raised a difficult question. They asked if negotiation and compromise may be necessary to secure your mother Daw Aung San Suu Kyi’s release. How would you respond to that?
Kim Aris: Well, I realize there are people who have been calling for my mother’s release all the time for the last five years, and without their support, I wouldn’t even have gotten this far. And people do have to negotiate—that’s very clear. At the same time, they should not be legitimizing the military by open discussions like this and welcoming Min Aung Hlaing to their country without actually having secured progress.
RFA: After hearing your mother’s voice for the first time in more than five years, what message would you like to share with the Myanmar people or international community?
Kim Aris: Well, I would say she is sounding well and strong still, but at 81 years old and with ongoing health concerns, and we still don’t know what conditions she’s really been kept under, I’d ask for everybody to continue to fight for her freedom. Burma needs to come forwards, and may may is part of that process still. People need to talk to one another, and one of the few people who is actually able to get people to talk to one another is may may . So please, do not stop fighting for her freedom. Fighting for her freedom is also fighting for the freedom of Burma.
Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: Aung San Suu Kyi phone call is ‘political calculation’ by military-backed government
articles.excerpt: Advocates demand full release of Myanmar's former leader after her first contact with family in 5 years.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Burmese
Updated 5:05 PM ET
Allowing Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi to speak on the phone with her son for the first time in five years is not enough – the military government must immediately release her and all other political prisoners, a human rights advocate told Radio Free Asia Thursday.
The country’s military-backed government announced that the former leader – currently under house arrest – was allowed to talk for 20 minutes to her son Kim Aris at 2:30 p.m. via a call placed to the Myanmar embassy in London, where Aris resides.
The chance to talk to her son came just days after the military released images of her receiving a letter and some books sent by Britain’s King Charles III.
In this image released by the Myanmar government, Aung San Suu Kyi's son, Kim Aris, at the Myanmar embassy in London talks on the phone with his mother, in Naypyidaw, Myanmar, Oct. 22, 2026.
(Myanmar Presidential Spokesman via Reuters) While the phone call was a joyous occasion for mother and son, much more must be done to bring peace to Myanmar, Aung Myo Kyaw, an official with the Thailand-based Assistance Association for Political Prisoners (AAPP), told RFA.
“Aung San Suu Kyi is not only a mother to Kim, but also a mother to the country,” said Aung Myo Kyaw. “What the citizens of the country need is the release of all political prisoners, including Aung San Suu Kyi.”
He said that the gradual easing of restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi is a political calculation by the military government, which he said was failing in all aspects.
At a time when the military continues to airstrike populated areas of the country, simply allowing her to talk to her son in the U.K. will not bring peace, he said.
“FREE HER. FREE THEM ALL”
In an interview with Radio Free Asia after speaking with his mother, Kim Aris said that it’s clear that the Myanmar military-backed government have been trying to “be more appealing to the international community.”
“But people need to remember that the military haven’t actually abided by any of what they have said they will have done over the last five years,” Aris told RFA. “They have not met the five-point consensus, and yet people are starting to re-engage with them without having seen any evidence of actual progress.”
In a Facebook post, Aris said that he was glad to finally hear his mother’s voice again and thanked supporters for continuing to advocate for her freedom.
But he reiterated that she is still “unjustly detained.”
“One conversation is not regular family access. Family access is not freedom,” he said. “My mother must never be used as a hostage or bargaining chip for diplomatic recognition, sanctions relief or political advantage.”
He called on governments that engage with Myanmar’s military authorities to not legitimize them in exchange for humanitarian rights.
“My mother and all political prisoners must be released immediately and unconditionally. Freedom is not negotiable. Accountability Before Legitimacy. FREE HER. FREE THEM ALL,” he wrote.

Aung San Suu Kyi has been detained since the 2021 military coup that ousted her and the rest of the country’s democratically elected government from power. She was sentenced to 18 years for a broad range of crimes that include corruption and election fraud, though she maintains that she is innocent.
For the duration of her detention, her exact location has not been easy to ascertain, and in April the military government moved her into house arrest . Until the brief phone call with her son Thursday, she had had almost no contact with the outside.
Radio Free Asia attempted to contact a spokesman for the military government to discuss more details about the phone call between Aung San Suu Kyi and Kim Aris, but there was no response.
Updates with Kim Aris comment from RFA interview.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Duterte impeachment: bribing elites is China’s strategy, military official says
articles.excerpt: Philippine government launches national security probes into Chinese influence.
articles.fullText:
MANILA - If Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte accepted funds from Beijing to grant political favors, it would fall directly within standard operating procedures for Chinese foreign influence operations, a Philippine military official told Radio Free Asia.
The remarks came after prosecutors in the vice president’s impeachment trial presented evidence of the alleged corruption – a financial forensics accountant testified that Cale88 Foods Corp., controlled by Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio, received 319 million pesos (US$5 million) from state-run Chinese firms. Duterte said the allegations were politically motivated.
The revelations raised alarm bells, with Filipino officials and experts immediately raising the specter of Chinese spy and malign influence operations as the two countries have become locked in an increasingly tense territorial dispute in the South China Sea, parts of which are claimed by Manila and referred to as the West Philippine Sea.
The competing claims in the South China Sea.
(RFA) Gaining access to the most influential people in a target country is a fundamental malign influence strategy for Beijing, retired Rear Adm. Roy Vincent Trinidad, spokesman for the Philippine military in the West Philippine Sea, told RFA.
“Part of the rulebook of the Chinese Communist Party includes economic elite co-optation and political elite co-optation,” Trinidad told RFA. “If they could co-opt a political leader, have him elected by building him up politically through foreign malign influence, they would have achieved the objective without firing a single shot.”
While donations or grants by any government are not illegal per se and are governed by rules, if the supposed investments are “used to advance the position of our adversary…it will have very serious national security implications,” Trinidad said.
“When another country would like to occupy your territory, would like to sow false narratives to advance their interests, they are creating trouble not only domestically, but in the region,” he stressed.
Going bananas?
Duterte was impeached in May for large-scale corruption and death threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., her former political ally turned nemesis.
The prosecution on Oct. 13 dropped three of the charges – misuse of funds, bribery, and grave threats – to speed up the trial, but she still remains accused of having unexplained wealth.
During the trial proceedings earlier in the month, the Anti-Money Laundering Council said the funds paid to the food company controlled by Duterte and her husband were in suspiciously high amounts for what they had been reported as – payment for banana chips, and that the firm did not have the operational capabilities that matched those payments.
Banana chips are displayed at a food show in Paris, Oct. 20, 2014.
(Bertrand Guay/AFP) The defense cited customs records that showed outgoing banana chip shipments with a declared value of 217 million pesos ($3.4 million), which is still about 100 million pesos less than the payments received.
Additionally, the trial revealed that the company had only two employees, which Senator-Judge Joel Villanueva during the proceedings said was “alarming” considering the company’s reported revenue and sales.
Government officials cannot be the direct beneficiary of funds from any foreign government, Leila de Lima, one of the prosecutors in Duterte’s impeachment trial, told RFA. She called the case a “substantiation of financial infusion by China” to influence.
“VP Sara’s receipt of funds from China without any exempting justification such as a legitimate business squarely constitutes a betrayal of her oath and disloyalty to the Philippines,” she said. “There can only be one reason for the receipt of hundreds of millions of pesos in monetary benefits by a public official from a foreign government.”
China’s Embassy in Manila did not immediately respond when contacted by RFA. But in a short statement it issued on Oct. 5, the embassy urged “relevant individuals in the Philippines to stop political manipulation and not drag Philippine domestic politics into China-Philippine relations.”
“A serious matter”
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., talking to reporters during a visit to Singapore on Oct. 11, acknowledged that the prosecution’s allegations were a “serious matter” that needed to be investigated.
If found to be true “it would go straight to the top of our list of threats that are facing the Philippines,” Marcos said, according to official transcripts of his interview with the traveling Filipino press.
“We are talking about the sovereignty of the Republic,” he said. “We are talking about the safety and security of the state. And I cannot think of any discussion that occurs at a higher level than that.”
Following Marcos’ statement, the National Security Council as well as state intelligence units were tasked to probe deeper into the allegations. The council said it took the allegations very seriously at a time of increased Chinese intelligence operations locally.
“The reported transactions and any credible information involving significant financial flows that may bear upon the country’s national security warrants careful, in-depth and responsible assessment,” national security adviser Eduardo Oban told reporters. He said the NSC will work with other agencies to assess “national security implications, if any, arising from the reported transactions.”
Alleged Chinese spy operations have been documented in the Philippines, and defense and national security officials are working to weed out Filipinos compromised by Chinese operatives. Earlier this year, RFA interviewed one of three Filipinos recently caught spying for China , who explained he had been recruited through an online advertisement.
"Danny," a Filipino who spied for China, talks to RFA at an undisclosed location in Manila, Philippines in April 2026.
(Jason Gutierrez/RFA) The military is in the process of weeding out more alleged spies through an “insider threat program” launched in 2023 and designed to protect sensitive government information, including data linked to the South China Sea.
After Marcos’ remarks, Vice President Duterte dismissed the allegations against her as political theatrics meant to target and harass her family through surveillance. “And this could have serious implications to our relationship with China,” she said.
Duterte is the daughter of former President Rodrigo Duterte, whose six-year term ended in 2022. During his presidency, the elder Duterte pursued a conciliatory stance toward Beijing—a sharp contrast to Marcos, who has leaned heavily into a U.S.-aligned foreign policy.
The younger Duterte joined forces with Marcos – himself the son of a former president – during the 2022 campaign to form an unbeatable UniTeam ticket that united the country’s two most powerful political dynasties.
The alliance between two of the leading political families in the country however soon crumbled, with Marcos in 2025 allowing the International Criminal Court to arrest Rodrigo Duterte for deaths related to his war on drugs.
Officials told RFA they would continue their operations against foreign operatives known to operate in the country. On Oct. 12, the military said its intelligence operatives helped immigration officials in raiding a hub for online gaming operations near military headquarters, and arrested 76 individuals, mostly Chinese nationals.
Operatives told RFA that the raid was part of its program to disrupt Chinese spying and malign influence operations, but declined to elaborate citing the sensitivity of the ongoing investigation.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: China-Laos air base could be another Southeast Asian forward outpost for Beijing
articles.excerpt: Like Ream Naval Base in Cambodia, Ban Keun could lay the groundwork for increased Chinese presence, analysts said.
articles.fullText:
A new joint military training facility in Laos could give Beijing a lasting foothold in mainland Southeast Asia even without an immediate boost to its combat power, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
Beijing and Vientiane opened a joint support and training center and an aviation academy at Ban Keun, about 50 kilometers north of the Lao capital, on Sept. 29. Beijing says the facility will train Lao air force pilots and it will be maintained by both countries.
The airfield, once complete, would be China’s second joint military outpost in Southeast Asia, after a Chinese-funded expansion of Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base opened in April of last year. The facility at Ream, despite its official designation as a dual-use facility, has seen a regular rotation of Chinese naval vessels.
The joint facility in Laos could allow China to deepen military ties, familiarize personnel with overseas operations and lay the groundwork for a larger presence, Joseph Kristanto, a research analyst at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, told RFA.
“Ultimately, I think the more important question is not simply whether Ban Keun could accommodate Chinese military aircraft, but whether Beijing intends to develop the facility into a sustained operational hub,” he said.
China’s Defense Ministry said in an announcement that the facility would be maintained by both countries and was “not directed against any third party.” It said its construction and use complied with domestic and international law and would strengthen military cooperation and support regional peace and stability.
Laos’ state news agency KPL reported that officials from both countries described the project at the opening ceremony as the product of cooperation based on mutual respect and equality. The facility would develop Lao military pilots’ practical skills, it said.
The locations of Ban Keun Airfield in Laos and Ream Naval Base in Cambodia.
(RFA) The KPL report also said both sides pledged to expand cooperation through joint training and exercises, personnel development and humanitarian assistance. Neither that report nor the Chinese announcement specified how many Chinese military personnel would work at Ban Keun, how long they would remain or the conditions governing Chinese aircraft deployments.
Satellite imagery analysis provided to RFA suggests some construction continued after the opening of the joint airfield. But its future military significance will depend on more than its physical completion, including the extent of Chinese access and the frequency and nature of activities there, Kristanto said.
China already operates military facilities on disputed features in the South China Sea. Ban Keun could extend its overseas presence inland, offering opportunities to build closer ties with the Lao military and gain experience operating from a foreign facility, he said.
The airfield’s immediate military advantages are less clear, analysts said. China has airbases in its own southern territory closer to the South China Sea, raising questions about what additional operations an inland facility in Laos would enable.
Strategic advantage for Beijing?
In satellite imagery of the airfield during its opening, eight aircraft are visible. Private satellite imagery analyst Jacob Bogle told RFA they were K-8, also known as JL-8, light attack and training aircraft.
Chinese JL-8 planes perform maneuvers in southern China's Guangdong province Sept. 28, 2021.
(Noel Celis/AFP) Examining an Oct. 7 image, he identified what he thought was one remaining aircraft, while cautioning that the image was blurry. He suggested the others had likely moved into hangars, although their locations could not be established from that observation.
Bogle also identified what appeared to be workshops and temporary construction infrastructure beside the southern end of the runway.
“So while the runway and main buildings are completed, it looks like there is still some minor work that is being finished,” he said.
The imagery does not establish who owns or operates the aircraft. Both China and Laos operate the K-8 type, according to analysts cited by Reuters.
But a Lao military officer, while downplaying concerns over increased Chinese military presence in Southeast Asia, confirmed to RFA that at least some of the fighter jets at the facility are Chinese.
“It is a pilot training airport. A group of people are envious that Laos has a flight training center, yet Laos has never complained about neighboring countries hosting U.S. air bases,” said the officer on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak on such matters.
“When Laos built Ban Keun Airport for pilot training, some people overreacted. Naturally, Chinese officials brought their own fighter jets, given that it is a joint Lao-Chinese operation,” he said.
Bogle said it was too early to determine China’s future position at Ban Keun, but that the facility warranted monitoring.
This satellite image taken Oct. 7, 2026, shows that previously visible aircraft have likely been moved into their hangars. Next to the southern end of the runway are what looks like workshops and other temporary construction infrastructure.
(RFA) Kristanto said operating combat aircraft from Laos would require substantial investment in fuel storage, maintenance facilities, munitions, air defense and other supporting infrastructure.
“At present, I see little evidence that Ban Keun offers a decisive operational advantage over China’s existing facilities,” he said.
Such limitations do not rule out a broader role in the future. Ban Keun could theoretically support intelligence gathering, surveillance, logistics or forward aircraft deployments if the necessary infrastructure and access arrangements were established, he said.
Surrounding Vietnam?
A sustained Chinese military presence in Laos could add another consideration for neighboring Vietnam, which already faces China across its northern land border and contests Beijing’s claims in the South China Sea.
China’s expansive maritime claims overlap with the exclusive economic zones of Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia. Vietnam also claims the Paracel and Spratly island groups, where competing sovereignty claims are distinct from disputes over rights to surrounding waters. China controls the Paracels, while several governments occupy features in the Spratlys.
In 2016, an international arbitral tribunal rejected China’s claims to the entire South China Sea based on its controversial nine-dash line, which surrounds the whole sea. This claim was seen to exceed what Beijing could legally claim under the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Credit: RFA
Beijing rejected the decision, and has continued to assert its claims over areas that are within the exclusive economic zones of the other claimants.
China has strengthened this position through island-building and military infrastructure, including runways, surveillance equipment and air defenses on occupied reefs. Those facilities support a wider maritime presence in waters where rival claimants seek to protect fishing grounds, energy resources and access to their outposts.
Ban Keun would introduce a different geographic consideration for Hanoi, potentially bringing Chinese military activity to its western side as well.
Bogle argued that facilities in Laos and Cambodia, together with China’s South China Sea bases, had effectively encircled Vietnam.
Kristanto was more cautious. Vietnam would have to account for the possibility of a Chinese military presence beyond its northern border and the South China Sea, he said, but Ban Keun’s inland location and China’s existing airbases limit its immediate operational value.
“For now, I would characterize Ban Keun as a potentially important strategic foothold rather than a major shift in the regional military balance.”
Ream offers a comparison
China’s involvement at Cambodia’s Ream naval base shows why a facility’s use over time can be more revealing than its designation as a joint training center, the analysts said.
China financed an expansion of Ream, on Cambodia’s southern coast, where its joint support and training center opened in April 2025. Cambodia maintains that Chinese personnel and warships are not permanently based there.
An analysis published in May 2025 by the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative documented Chinese naval vessels rotating through Ream after their initial arrival in December 2023.
Chinese navy vessels are clearly visible at Ream Naval Base, Cambodia. The Chinese navy appears to have kept a near permanent presence at the base ever since December 2023, after the "Chinese pier" was completed.
(RFA) It also found that visiting Japanese and Vietnamese vessels used a different waterfront area from the large pier occupied by Chinese ships, suggesting unequal access to some facilities. Those findings described arrangements at the time and do not establish current access rules.
Kristanto said the comparison with Ban Keun was useful in examining how China could expand its military presence through partnerships that initially fall short of large, permanent bases.
“Rather than immediately establishing large, permanent military bases, Beijing appears to be pursuing arrangements that could provide access, logistical support, and opportunities for a more sustained military presence.”
The differences remain substantial. Ream provides direct access to the sea and can support naval deployments, while Ban Keun’s military utility depends heavily on the aircraft and supporting infrastructure deployed there, he added.
For the Lao facility, subsequent construction and deployments will help establish whether the training partnership develops into a broader operational role.
“Its future significance will depend on the extent of Chinese access, the infrastructure developed, and the frequency and nature of PLA activities there,” Kristanto said.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Rare photos of Aung San Suu Kyi spark renewed calls for her release
articles.excerpt: Myanmar military releases images of jailed former leader receiving books and letters from Britain’s King Charles.
articles.fullText:
Myanmar’s military-backed government released images of deposed former leader Aung San Suu Kyi receiving items sent by King Charles III of the United Kingdom, a development that brought on renewed calls for the ousted former leader’s release.
Aung San Suu Kyi has been detained since the 2021 military coup that ousted her and the rest of the country’s democratically elected government from power. She was sentenced to 18 years for a broad range of crimes that include corruption and election fraud, though she maintains that she is innocent.
For the duration of her detention, her exact location has not been easy to ascertain.
The military government moved her to house arrest in April, but still have allowed almost no contact with the outside.
Aung San Suu Kyi received an envelope that contained diplomatic communication, and two books from King Charles – “The Land Gardeners: Soil to Table” and “Soil: The ​World at Our Feet.”
The delivery – which the military government revealed in a public statement – lasted only 10 minutes. It is the first acknowledgement of the detained former leader receiving correspondence from abroad.
Family members, Myanmar watchers and world government officials told RFA that they were pleased to know she was allowed to receive the king’s message, but they warned against allowing the military to use the delivery as propaganda.
Kim Aris, the younger son of Aung San Suu Kyi, told RFA that he took comfort that his mother was in the king’s thoughts and that he appreciated the kind gesture.
“I take comfort in knowing that my mother remains in the thoughts of His Majesty King Charles III, and I sincerely appreciate his kind gesture in sending her books. However, we must not allow the military regime to use such selective disclosures to create an illusion of normality or gain international legitimacy. A gesture of kindness should never be used to distract from the continued violation of my mother’s fundamental human rights. My mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, is an 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize laureate who remains unjustly detained on politically motivated charges, hidden from the world and denied direct contact with her family and independent medical assessment. Despite recent developments, we still have no direct communication with her or credible, independently verified information about her health and wellbeing. I hope His Majesty’s thoughtful gesture will also serve as a reminder to world leaders that my mother’s situation remains unresolved. I urge all governments engaging with Min Aung Hlaing to insist on meaningful humanitarian progress, including regular, direct family contact, independent medical access, and her immediate and unconditional release, together with all political prisoners.”
Cara Chittenden, a communications officer at the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, told RFA that Aung San Suu Kyi should not be in detention.
“The UK continues to condemn the arbitrary detention of Aung San Suu Kyi and calls for her immediate and unconditional release, alongside all those arbitrarily detained in Myanmar. We remain gravely concerned about her continued detention and wellbeing. The UK has also co-sponsored a number of Human Rights Council resolutions on Myanmar, including most recently in March 2026 . The resolution condemned human rights violations against the people of Myanmar, including the Rohingya and other ethnic minorities.”
A spokesperson from the U.S. Department of State said that Washington remained “concerned about all individuals unjustly detained” and continued “to call for their release and the military to engage in genuine dialogue with all opposition groups to end the conflict in Burma. The United States remains steadfast in our support for the people of Burma.”
Aung Myo Kyaw, a spokesperson from the Thailand-based Assistance Association for Political Prisoners, told RFA that the delivery of the books and letters was a positive development.
“However, the world does not view Aung San Suu Kyi as a ‘special prisoner,’ as the regime claims (in its statement); rather, she is recognized as a national leader. Whenever the military junta faces crises on various fronts, they tend to use Daw Aung San Suu Kyi as a hidden political card. In this instance, too, their actions are merely a gesture—a performance intended to project themselves as flexible and big-hearted.”
Kyaw Htwe, an exiled member of the Central Working Committee of Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy party, told RFA that the meeting was the military engaging in political theater.
“Engagement should be measured by political progress. When they fail to bring about such political progress, they typically resort to their usual tactic: releasing news regarding our Chairperson, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, to manipulate the situation. Rather than just sending books or letters, it is necessary to allow her to meet with her family—specifically her younger son—as well as her legal team.”
That legal team is reportedly seeking to meet her in person since May 30 prison-to-private house transfer, sources close to the legal team told RFA. The legal team’s repeated requests to meet with her are ignored by military authorities.
Myint Htwe, a government leader in a part of the country not controlled by the military, said that the junta’s move to publicize the delivery was meant to try to gain legitimacy.
“These are just the same old tactics. The fact that they chose to issue a press statement—when they could have easily handled the matter quietly—suggests a softening of their stance. I interpret this as a deliberate attempt to signal—to put on full display—that they are treating a communication from the British monarch with great seriousness, as a legitimate government would. Furthermore, I see it as an effort to project the image of being a legitimate government to the rest of the world.”
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Uyghur activists urge Rubio to raise rights concerns with Central Asian officials
articles.excerpt: Uzbekistan trip is a chance to reassert U.S. moral leadership by pressing the C5 to protect Uyghur communities.
articles.fullText:
Uyghur advocates have urged U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to seek commitments not to deport Uyghurs to China and to protect them from Beijing’s transnational repression during his upcoming meetings with Central Asian officials, the leader of a prominent Uyghur rights organization told Radio Free Asia.
Rubio is leading a U.S. delegation of more than 200 business representatives and will arrive in Uzbekistan on Saturday for the first leg of a six-day trip that also includes two stops in India. While in Samarkand, he will attend the C5+1 ministerial meetings – with officials from the five Central Asian countries of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio boards a plane, Oct. 8, 2026, in Lisbon.
(Mark Schiefelbein/AP) According to the Washington-based Uyghur Human Rights Project, more than 400,000 Uyghurs live in these Central Asian countries and combined they form the “vast majority” of the Uyghur diaspora outside of East Turkestan, which is the name by which Uyghurs call their homeland, currently under the control of the People’s Republic of China.
As a U.S. senator, Rubio was a champion of Uyghur issues and now as Washington’s top diplomat, he is expected to discuss the safety and rights of Uyghurs with the C5 leaders, Abdureshit Abdulhamit, vice president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress, told RFA.
Abdureshit Abdulhamit, vice president of the World Uyghur Congress.
(RFA Illustration) “We urge him to seek clear commitments that no Uyghur will be forcibly returned to China, where they could face persecution, imprisonment or torture,” said Abdureshit. “Uyghurs seeking protection should have access to fair asylum procedures.”
He also urged Rubio to address intimidation and surveillance targeting Uyghur communities, saying people should be able to preserve their culture, discuss detained relatives and communicate abroad without fear.
Communities at risk
Compared to Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, Uyghurs in Uzbekistan face more challenges to their social and cultural rights, Zumretay Erkin, another vice president of the organization, told RFA.
“Uzbekistan is also complicit in deporting Uyghurs to China at the explicit request of the Chinese government,” she said. “Uyghurs are subjected to tight surveillance and transnational repression.”
Zumretay Erkin, vice president of the World Uyghur Congress.
(RFA Illustration) Zumretay said Rubio’s diplomatic visit is a “unique opportunity to raise Uyghur human rights, even in a trade and investment context,” noting that the U.S. government was among the first to take action to address the Uyghur genocide.
Washington classified China’s treatment of Uyghurs in the Uyghur region as genocide in 2021.
Moral leadership
Rubio can show the world that the United States’ moral leadership still matters, Omer Kanat, executive director of the Washington-based Uyghur Human Rights Project, wrote in an opinion piece in The Diplomat.
Kanat cited former U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo’s public calls against returning Uyghurs to China as a precedent. He also pointed to Thailand’s February 2025 deportation of 40 Uyghurs as a warning of the consequences when diplomatic efforts fail.
Omer Kanat, executive director of the Uyghur Human Rights Project.
(RFA Illustration) “This upcoming trip to Central Asia gives Rubio a chance to show that the United States won’t countenance a repeat of that tragedy,” he wrote. “With the right messaging, the trip can fortify China’s neighbors to stand firm against Beijing’s pressure to return Uyghurs to China.”
The WUC also called on Rubio to hear directly from Uyghur representatives and establish follow-up mechanisms for individual cases.
“We would judge the visit by concrete results: stronger protection against deportation, action on cases of harassment and a clear American commitment to follow through after the meetings end,” said Abdureshit.
Edited by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Tibetan rights group: South Africa arson attack is transnational repression by CCP
articles.excerpt: Police are still investigating the firebombing of the Dalai Lama representative’s home office in South Africa.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Tibetan.
Authorities are still investigating Wednesday’s firebombing of the Dalai Lama’s representative office in South Africa, police told Radio Free Asia, as activists accused China of having a hand in the attack.
'Transnational repression' by China, Tibet activists say
The office of the Tibetan spiritual leader in Pretoria suffered extensive damage in the 11 p.m. attack, but nobody was hurt, the representative Dhondup Gyalpo told RFA.
“I heard the sound of breaking glass and saw smoke coming into the house. As soon as I realized what was happening, I broke a window and got outside,” he said. “Another firebomb that had not exploded was hanging above the window. I was slightly injured by broken glass.”
A fire burns at the residence and office of Dhondup Gyalpo, the Dalai Lama’s representative in South Africa, in Lyttelton Manor, Centurion, outside Pretoria, Oct. 14, 2026.
(Dhondup Gyalpo) Shortly after the fire brigade extinguished the blaze, the crime scene experts and detectives arrived to investigate, but no suspects have been arrested,” police spokesperson Brigadier BM Muridili, told RFA.
Wednesday’s firebombing was the second such attack on the office in months. The office had previously been firebombed in July, on the Dalai Lama’s 91st birthday. Gyalpo described Wednesday’s attack in detail.
“The Molotov cocktail used in the attack produced more smoke than flames. At first, it looked as though the entire building was on fire,” he said. “When I entered, the smoke was so thick and overpowering that I could almost taste it.”
The fire engulfed parts of the property, causing extensive damage to the building, furniture and official documents, he said. Neither Gyalpo nor Khenpo Jamyang Gonpo, a staff member at the office, was injured in the fire.
“Transnational repression”
The attacks on the Dalai Lama’s office are part of a “global rise in transnational repression” by the Chinese Communist Party against the Tibetan people, the New York-based rights group Students for a Free Tibet said in a statement.
“Students for a Free Tibet urges South African law enforcement and government authorities to conduct an immediate, thorough, and independent investigation,” the group said. “Law enforcement must not dismiss these attacks as ordinary local crime, but must explicitly examine political motives and potential foreign state involvement.”
The Desmond & Leah Tutu Legacy Foundation also condemned Wednesday’s attack in a statement and called for stronger protections of freedom of expression, religion and association.
Desmond Tutu and the Dalai Lama are both Nobel laureates for their nonviolent struggles, and in the statement, the foundation noted their long friendship.
The Dalai Lama speaks with Archbishop Desmond Tutu in Seattle, April 15, 2008.
(Ted S. Warren/AP) “We stand with the Tibetan community in South Africa and with everyone who lives and works at the Office,” the foundation said. “No community in South Africa should have to go to sleep wondering whether their home will be set alight because of who they are, where they come from or what they believe.”
Gyalpo said he suspected that the attack might be politically motivated, but cautioned that the perpetrators and their motives have not been identified yet.
“There seems to be a warning sign intended to intimidate us but we are not scared,” he said. “We have no reason to hate the people of South Africa and there is also no reason why the people of South Africa should not like us,” he said.
Edited by Tawang in Tibetan and Eugene Whong and Charlie Dharapak in English.

articles.title: China covered up the cause of a detained Uyghur father’s death
articles.excerpt: Police confirm to RFA that Yasinjan Toxti died in their custody in 2018, not in a traffic accident.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Uyghur
Chinese authorities in 2018 lied to the family of a Uyghur bus driver who died in their custody, an investigation by Radio Free Asia has revealed.
Authorities told the family of Yasinjan Toxti, who had been detained in a “re-education” facility on suspicion of “religious radicalism,” that he had died in a car accident.
Yasinjan’s sister Reyhangul told RFA that the details did not add up. A resident of Belgium, Reyhangul discussed the moment in 2018 when her younger sister in the Uyghur region told her of her brother’s death.
“How could someone held in ‘re-education’ die in a traffic accident?” she recalled asking. She said her sister replied, “That is what the police told us. We have to accept that explanation. Under the current circumstances, we cannot ask any further questions about it.”
2018 was the height of China’s Uyghur internment campaign aimed at “curbing terrorism” where an estimated 1.8 million Uyghurs were put in detainment facilities claimed by authorities to be vocational training centers. The U.S. in 2020 classified Beijing’s actions in the Uyghur region as a genocide.
Inconsistencies uncovered
In an attempt to gain more clarity on the circumstances of Yasinjan’s death, RFA this month telephoned the Qartal Bazaar police station in Aksu, an oasis city in the Uyghur region, where Yasinjan lived and worked.
Two separate police personnel shared information that conflicted with what authorities told Reyhangul’s family in 2018.
The chief of the police station was the first to answer RFA’s questions.
RFA spoke to the chief of police in Aksu, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
(RFA Illustration) A police officer on duty provided further details.
RFA spoke to a police officer in Aksu, Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
(RFA Illustration) In assessing that Yasinjan had been in detention for “five or six months,” the police chief may have been referring to his cumulative time in re-education across multiple sentences, and the police officer who said he was taken to the hospital after “nine or 10 days” may have been referring to the length of time into his latest sentence. RFA was unable to confirm what either expression of time meant exactly.
Educational pursuits
Yasinjan was born in 1980 in Aksu and lived there his entire life. Having received only a primary school education himself, Yasinjan saw the importance of education and sent his five-year-old son, Hebibulla Yasin, to study in Egypt. His sister was already living in Egypt overseeing her own children’s education, and agreed to be Hebibulla’s caretaker there.
Sending children abroad for educational purposes was at the time common for many Uyghur families, because China had been expanding its policy of “bilingual education,” – which in practice was replacing the Uyghur language with Mandarin Chinese for most classes.
Many Uyghur parents viewed this as accelerating assimilation, and feared their children would lose their Uyghur cultural and religious identity. Egypt, which had a strong reputation for Islamic education, and relatively low living costs, was a natural choice for families wishing to preserve their culture.
Before 2017, more than 5,000 Uyghurs were living in Egypt, but mass arrests by the Chinese government under the “Strike Hard Campaign Against Violent Terrorism” intensified the next year . Arrests often targeted Uyghurs with family members abroad, especially in “sensitive” Muslim majority countries like Turkey and Egypt.
Arousing suspicion
Because his son was in Egypt, Yasinjan was detained several times between 2016 and 2018 on suspicion of “religious radicalism” and subjected to short periods of “re-education,” according to Reyhangul. Authorities were able to compel Yasinjan to bring Hebibulla home, but even after his son returned, Yasinjan remained under suspicion.
Yasinjan was in custody four separate times between 2016 and 2018. His latest detention was for stopping the bus in the middle of his route to allow Muslim passengers to observe the call to prayer.
It was during this latest detention that he died – not of a traffic accident as Reyhangul said authorities previously claimed – but after arriving in a “re-education camp” as confirmed by police in RFA’s investigation.
Years after Yasinjan’s death, while Reyhangul was searching for more information, she learned that other members of her family had been detained – her sister, who had told her about their brother’s death, for “leaking state secrets,” and her mother, who had traveled to Turkey, for “visiting a sensitive country.”
Still, Reyhangul does not know where they are detained, nor the length of their sentences, she said.
Edited by Eugene Whong and Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: MPF schemes notice published
articles.excerpt: The Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes (General) (Amendment) Regulation 2025 will come into operation on December 21, following a notice published…
articles.fullText:
The Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes (General) (Amendment) Regulation 2025 will come into operation on December 21, following a notice published today in the Government Gazette.

This commencement notice facilitates the rollout of Phase One of Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) "Full Portability". Under the Amendment Regulation, employees whose employment began on or after May 1 last year (New EEs) will be permitted to transfer the entirety of their accrued benefits derived from employer mandatory contributions in respect of their current employment.

These funds can be moved from the employer’s chosen MPF scheme to a personal account of an MPF scheme of their own choice. Transfers can be made once every calendar year, or more frequently if permitted by the governing rules of the transferring MPF scheme.

Secretary for Financial Services & the Treasury Christopher Hui stated that with the implementation of Phase One "Full Portability" on December 21, the Government has fulfilled its commitment outlined in the 2026 Policy Address. He noted that this change will give new employees greater control over their MPF benefits, encourage more proactive management of their investments, stimulate market competition, and create room for fee reductions.

Mr Hui added that the Government is currently drafting legislative proposals for Phase Two "Full Portability", which will extend these benefits to the remaining workforce. The corresponding amendment bill is scheduled to be introduced to the Legislative Council by mid-2027.

The commencement notice will be tabled before the Legislative Council next Wednesday for negative vetting.

articles.title: China’s TNR: Three communities, three phases, one evolving system
articles.excerpt: RFA convened a closed, bipartisan roundtable on Capitol Hill, “China’s Transnational Repression (TNR)
articles.fullText:
WASHINGTON—Ahead of Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, D.C. in September, Radio Free Asia (RFA) convened a closed, bipartisan roundtable on Capitol Hill, “China’s Transnational Repression (TNR): Three Communities, Three Phases, One Evolving System”—examining trends and developments regarding the targeting of Tibetan, Uyghur, and Hong Kong diaspora communities and groups. RFA, uniquely positioned to host the roundtable, has both documented TNR’s rise and has been a target.
From that discussion with Congressional staff, policymakers, rights advocates, academics, and journalists, RFA is reporting out a set of recommendations and ideas regarding TNR’s development, growth, and sophistication. Issues raised were ways of protecting journalists and advocates, TNR’s use by Beijing as a tactic aimed at manipulating global narratives, artificial intelligence’s role in expanding its scope, its growing presence on U.S. soil , including universities and diaspora communities, and Beijing’s growing influence with international institutions, such as Interpol, to aid its efforts.
“From RFA’s exclusive reporting on restrictions of religious freedom in Tibet and forced labor and human rights abuses in Xinjiang, to closing our physical bureau in Hong Kong after authorities enacted Article 23 and named us a ‘foreign force,’ RFA and our journalists have endured every iteration of TNR designed to silence us and inhibit transparency,” RFA President and CEO Bay Fang said.
Delivering opening remarks at the roundtable was Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR), former Chair of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC), who introduced the bipartisan Transnational Repression Policy Act (S.2525) last year, co-sponsored by current CECC Chair Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK). The conversation, moderated by RFA’s Chief Communications Officer Rohit Mahajan, delved into the issues outlined above, with an eye on fostering greater cross-sector cooperation, understanding, and solutions.
RFA plans to continue engaging on this issue with partners, policymakers, authorities, technologists, freedom advocates, journalists, and experts in this critical space.
Read the chief takeaways from RFA’s session here: https://docs.rfa.org/english/docs/RFA_TNR_Roundtable_Sept.2026.pdf .

articles.title: After US accuses Fijian of corruption for China, experts warn of region-wide network
articles.excerpt: “Illicit disruptors” in Pacific allow Beijing to benefit from illegal activity while offering plausible deniability
articles.fullText:
Beijing’s corruption and influence operations are not limited to Fiji, and similar operations likely exist in other Pacific island countries, experts on the region told Radio Free Asia.
The analysis came shortly after Washington accused Fijian national Zhao Fugang of corruption as head of the Overseas Chinese Service Center in Suva.
“Zhao abused his public position by paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance China-based government, business, and criminal interests,” U.S. State Department spokesman Thomas Pigott said in a statement. “His actions constituted significant corruption and adversely affected U.S. interests in Fiji.”
Though Zhao is now barred from entering the United States, there are probably more people involved in the type of corruption he is accused of – not just in Fiji, but across the entire Pacific region, Gregory Brown, executive director of the Washington-based Alliance Futures Initiative think tank, told RFA.
“I seriously doubt that Beijing set up a corruption and influence operation in Fiji and then decided not to replicate it anywhere else in a region where it’s spending billions on infrastructure, signing security agreements, and competing every day for political influence,” said Brown. “That defies logic and everything we know about the CCP’s overseas influence campaigns. There is no reason similar operations wouldn’t work in Honiara, Port Moresby, Nuku’alofa, or Port Vila.”
A map showing the location of Fiji within the Pacific region.
(AFP) Illicit activities that advance Chinese interests occur elsewhere in the Pacific, Kathryn Paik, deputy director of the Australia Chair at the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, told RFA.
“There have been many documented cases of Chinese actors in other Pacific countries and territories conducting illegal activities such as drug trafficking, illegal fishing, money laundering, and more,” said Paik. “What is key is that while most if not all of these actors may not be an official Chinese agent, they are conducting activity that is either encouraged by or facilitated by Beijing.”
Illicit disruptors
Zhao is an example of China’s use of “state-condoned illicit disruptors as a form of gray zone activity in the Pacific,” José Sousa-Santos, of the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, wrote in an essay published in Small Wars Journal , a project by the Future Security Initiative at Arizona State University.
Written months before the U.S. sanctioned Zhao – who Australian law enforcement had already identified as having connections to organized crime – the essay detailed how Beijing tolerates and protects criminal figures and networks to serve objectives of the state.
“This does not require a simple command relationship between the Chinese state and organized crime. Nor does it mean that every Chinese criminal actor abroad is an agent of Beijing,” wrote Sousa-Santos. “The more important point is that certain illicit actors can become strategically useful when they extend influence, cultivate local elites, generate deniable economic leverage, support patriotic narratives, and operate in spaces where formal state power would attract resistance.”
Actors like Zhao are valuable in that Beijing can deny all connections of involvement in their illegal activities, all while benefiting from them, the essay said.
“Zhao’s value is that he represents the kind of high-risk intermediary who can move money, cultivate elites, open doors, normalize Chinese influence, and generate dependency while remaining formally outside the state,” it said.
After the U.S. sanctioned Zhao, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a news conference she had no knowledge of his case.
“We oppose vilification and smears against China,” she said.
Cooperation needed
In a Facebook post, the Fijian government asked Washington to provide evidence of the allegations against Zhao, and affirmed Suva’s commitment to work with international partners to crack down on transnational crime.
The U.S. and its allies should coordinate with each other to stop illicit activities, Paik said.
“Working collaboratively to identify illegal activity and name specific actors is certainly a start,” she said. “But of course Pacific countries are sovereign nations and the next step will ideally be to take action against these individuals in whichever country they are acting.”
Brown said that the U.S. should not stop with its sanctions on Zhao, but should name other individuals in the region to demonstrate how widespread the problem is.
“If we see three or four more across different Pacific countries in the next six months, the signal becomes a pattern,” he said.
Brown also called for the U.S. and its allies to support Pacific governments in building their own anti-corruption and counter-intelligence capacity, urged Pacific governments to make foreign-linked community organizations more accountable by requiring them to register, and work together to protect Chinese diaspora communities in the region.
“My big question now is whether this designation is a one-off or a campaign,” he said. “If it’s a one-off, Beijing will absorb the hit and move on. If it’s a campaign, it’s a chance to change calculus for every Chinese operative and every compromised Pacific official in the region.”
Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: Kindergarten profiles released online
articles.excerpt: The Education Bureau today released the latest online profiles of local kindergartens and childcare centres to help parents make informed…
articles.fullText:
The Education Bureau today released the latest online profiles of local kindergartens and childcare centres to help parents make informed school choices for their children.

The dedicated website provides information on about 930 kindergartens and childcare centres in Hong Kong, including the approved fees for all kindergartens for the 2026-27 academic year. It also identifies kindergartens participating in the kindergarten education scheme.

The profiles display each institution's approved fees after government subsidies are deducted, alongside their official quality review results. Furthermore, parents can access details regarding the professional qualifications of staff and total numbers of teachers.

The website also features enrolment figures, teacher-to-pupil ratios, curriculum information, and reference prices for major education items, application and registration fees.

Additionally, the profiles include dedicated columns outlining the specific support available for non-Chinese speaking students, as well as the resources offered for children with special needs.

articles.title: Exclusive: North Korean army video says K-drama watchers deserve to be executed
articles.excerpt: Used in ideological training sessions, the video calls offenders as “traitors” who “gouged out their own eyes.”
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean
A North Korean video warns soldiers that they could be punished - and they should be executed - for watching foreign media, a recording obtained exclusively by Radio Free Asia reveals.
North Korean army video says K-drama watchers deserve to be executed
A female narrator with a booming voice denounces soldiers for not resisting the temptation to watch “impure recordings” like South Korean TV shows and Hollywood films.
The footage obtained by RFA is a recording of a screen showing the video. It is believed to have been produced in 2023 and is still in use in soldiers’ ideological training sessions, sources inside the country told RFA on condition of anonymity for security reasons.
“I strongly demand, on behalf of all military personnel, the summary execution of those who have become thoroughly steeped in the rotten imperialist ideology, culture and way of life,” the narrator says. She calls for the “relentless pursuit and capture” of those who watch foreign media so that they can be “subjected to merciless punishment.”
The educational video presents the cautionary tales of at least two military personnel who were caught watching foreign media, detailing how they were punished.
Media matters
North Korea routinely punishes citizens for watching foreign media or listening to foreign music which is typically smuggled into the country and distributed on thumb drives and easily concealable micro SD cards.
Distributing it can result in the death penalty . In one high profile case reported in 2021 by RFA, a man was sentenced to death for selling copies of the hit Netflix series “Squid Game.”
This image courtesy of Netflix shows a scene from South Korea's "Squid Game" season one.
(Youngkyu Park/Netflix via AFP) Offenders that merely watched foreign media – but did not distribute it – are usually given a lesser, but still harsh sentence in a labor camp. Parents can even be punished for the crimes of their children. Citizens can even be presumed guilty on tangential evidence – speaking like South Koreans or texting using South Korean spellings – habits they are presumed to have picked up from watching illegal videos from the South.
Despite the government’s efforts, including the passage in 2020 of the draconian Elimination of Reactionary Thought and Culture Law, which lays out specific punishments for foreign media-related crimes, North Koreans continue to tune in.
But members of the military are under even more scrutiny. A task force called the “109 Group” catches soldiers with surprise inspections, and after a soldier is caught , reports of punishments soon follow.
Because every North Korean spends seven to 10 years in the military after high school, the appetite for South Korean and U.S. media among soldiers is quite high, Yoshihiro Makino, a diplomatic correspondent for the Asahi Shimbun newspaper in Japan and a visiting professor at Hiroshima University, told RFA.
“With so many young people gathered in one organization, it is impossible to say that none of them are interested in that kind of culture,” Makino said.
Footage of a North Korean educational propaganda video shows a soldier arrested for watching illegal foreign media.
(RFA Korean) He added that it is not common in North Korea to see public accounts of military trials, because of the need to protect military secrets, so the fact that the proceedings are shown in the educational video indicates that authorities are concerned about the spread of South Korean culture, which they refer to as ideological contamination.
“Puppet-trash culture”
The educational video continues by showing several people in courtrooms being cuffed and led away as the narrator chastises foreign media watchers for being infected by the culture of the “puppets” of the United States – an oft-used pejorative referring to South Koreans. She calls these people “weeds of our society” and “trash of our era.”
She then blames the U.S. and South Korea for spreading “rotten capitalist and puppet-trash culture on a massive scale,” and complains about sanctions aimed at depriving Pyongyang of cash and resources that could be funneled into its nuclear and missile programs, calling them a U.S. “strangulation campaign.”
Against this backdrop she asks if watching foreign media could be anything but treason.
“Are not those infected by the political poison spread by the enemy a band of traitors acting as one with our principal enemies, and poisonous mushrooms that must be uprooted entirely?”
The narrator goes on to remind soldiers that they aren’t supposed to use civilian mobile phones, with the video showing examples of smartphones and flip phones that authorities confiscated.
Footage of a North Korean educational propaganda video shows mobile phones confiscated from soldiers.
(RFA Korean) “Soldiers performing individual duties, including drivers of passenger vehicles, purchased, watched, stored and distributed impure recordings through civilian mobile phones,” the narrator says. “In the end, these phones led them down the path of treason and counterrevolution, ruining their lives.”
A second video file obtained by RFA, containing footage of a later section of the educational video, discusses the case of Kim Kye Hyang, a military doctor punished for watching foreign media.
“The Party educated … and even appointed her as a military doctor in the revolutionary army,” an on-camera military official says. “But look at what happened. Watching impure recordings turned her, at the very beginning of her life, into an ungrateful and contemptible person.”
Footage of a North Korean educational propaganda video shows an “arrest warrant” for Kim Kye Hyang, a military doctor who watched illegal foreign media.
(RFA Korean) The official says her parents are now devastated and they cry often, wishing she had never been born. She denounces foreign recordings as a poison that wastes time, damages health and ruins the lives of offenders and their families.
The footage then shows a detained soldier writing a confession. Weeping, he says that watching foreign recordings “once or twice” gradually filled his mind with South Korean speech patterns and capitalist ideology.
“I deeply regret it,” he says while seemingly crying. With ominous music, the line is repeated several times with an eerie echo effect over a stopped frame of his anguished face.
A female soldier, clad in pink formal wear, appears next. She identifies the regretful soldier as Ju Chol Bom and says his case is proof that watching foreign media is “the path to ruining one’s life.”
The narrator also warns that such crimes are committed through personal connections and will eventually be exposed. The message appears to be that even if authorities do not detect an offense immediately, offenders can still be caught.
“Why do people realize the value of something precious only after losing it?” the speaker asks. “Ju Chol Bom’s fate clearly demonstrates that watching the enemy’s subversive footage, while knowing it is an act of treason and rebellion that dances to the enemy’s tune, is the very path to becoming the most foolish suicide victim in the world and ruining one’s own destiny.”
A male soldier then says that the offense deserves severe punishment and suggests that offenders not only harmed themselves, but others as well.
Footage of a North Korean educational propaganda video shows a North Korean soldier reading an arrest warrant in front of a soldier who was caught illegally watching foreign media.
(RFA Korean) “Ju Chol Bom and several other offenders received sentences of five or more years of hard labor,” the male soldier says. “Because watching impure recordings is a serious crime, even a general amnesty is not permitted. In the end, with their own hands, they gouged out their own eyes.”
The loud, overarticulate voice of the narrator continues, implying that the actions of Ju and those like him dragged down others.
“But their eyes are not the only ones gouged out …”
The footage of the video abruptly cuts out.
Edited in Korean by Yi Yongin and in English by Eugene Whong.

articles.title: Commentary: The story China wants you to swallow
articles.excerpt: China is marketing fish from Xinjiang as a triumph of technology and frontier development.
articles.fullText:
On May 22, 2018, China Central Television broadcast a glowing segment about salmon farming in western China. Over images of sleek fish cutting through clear water, the narrator marveled that “a precious fish like salmon, which typically lives in the open ocean,” could now be raised in the desert. Technology had made the improbable possible. “The land is the same land, and the people are the same people,” the program declared, “but when technology is brought in, miracles are born.”
Viewers were unconvinced and immediately began voicing skepticism about seafood coming from such a surprising place.
